bio.en: Cat Wu is Head of Product for Claude Code and Cowork at Anthropic, at the center of how AI is changing the way products are built.
bio.zh: Cat Wu 是 Anthropic 的 Claude Code 与 Cowork 产品负责人，正处于 AI 改变产品构建方式的核心。

summary.en: Cat argues the hardest part isn't building for a future superintelligent model but eliciting maximum capability from today's models, and that shipping timelines at Anthropic have collapsed from six months to as little as a day. She says the PM role is changing fast—what matters most now is product taste, since code is cheap and deciding what to build is the scarce skill. The conversation covers what emerging PM skills look like in an AI-native world.
summary.zh: Cat 认为，难点不在于为未来的超级智能模型构建，而在于从今天的模型中“逼出”最大能力，且 Anthropic 的功能交付周期已从六个月缩短到最短一天。她说 PM 角色正快速变化——如今最重要的是产品品味，因为代码廉价，而“决定造什么”才是稀缺技能。对话涵盖了在 AI 原生世界里新兴 PM 技能的样子。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: I think it is very hard to be the right amount of AGI-pilled. It's very easy to build the product for the super AGI strong model. The hard thing is figuring out for the current model, how do you elicit the maximum capability?
turns.zh: 我认为适量的 AGI 填充是非常困难的。构建超级 AGI 强模型的产品非常容易。困难的是弄清楚当前模型，如何获得最大能力？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've never seen anything like the pace folks at Anthropic are shipping at.
turns.zh: 我从来没有见过像 Anthropic 人员那样的发货速度。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: We want to remove every single barrier to shipping things. The timelines for a lot of our product features have gone down from six month to one month and sometimes to even one day.
turns.zh: 我们希望消除运输过程中的每一个障碍。我们许多产品功能的时间表已从六个月缩短到一个月，有时甚至缩短到一天。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're interviewing hundreds of PMs and you just keep feeling like they're approaching it very incorrectly.
turns.zh: 你正在面试数百名产品经理，但你总是感觉他们的处理方式非常错误。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: The PM role is changing a lot. It's changing really quickly. The thing that is extremely important for building AI-native products is iterating so quickly, figuring out a way for you to actually launch features every single week.
turns.zh: PM 的角色正在发生很大变化。它的变化真的很快。对于构建人工智能原生产品来说，极其重要的是快速迭代，找到一种方法让你每周都能真正推出功能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you think are the emerging skills PMs need to develop?
turns.zh: 您认为产品经理需要发展哪些新兴技能？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: It comes back to product taste. As code becomes much cheaper to write, the thing that becomes more valuable is deciding what to write.
turns.zh: 这又回到了产品的味道。随着代码的编写成本变得越来越低，决定编写什么内容变得更有价值。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: I think before AI, technology shifts were a lot slower, so you could plan on these six to 12 month time horizons, and because you were shipping features at a bit of a slower rate, there was a lot more emphasis on coordinating with all the other partner teams to make sure that their shipping features that unblock your features because code at that time was very expensive to make. I think now with AI and with how much that has accelerated engineering and with how quickly the model capabilities are improving, the timelines for a lot of our product features have gone down from six month to one month and sometimes to one week or even one day. And with that, we actually need to make sure that products ship quite quickly. (00:05:49): And what that means is as a PM, there should be less emphasis on making sure that you're aligning your multi-quarter roadmaps with your partner teams and more emphasis on, okay, how can we figure out the fastest way to get something out the door? How can we figure out how to make a concept corner of our product suite where we can just... An engineer has an idea or a PM has an idea, and by the end of the week, we are able to get into our user's hands. I think the PMs who do the best on AI-native products are the ones who can figure out, how can I shorten the time from having this idea to actually getting the product in the hands of users and help define what are the most important tasks that need to work out of the box for my product?
turns.zh: 我认为在人工智能出现之前，技术转变要慢得多，所以你可以在这六到十二个月的时间范围内进行计划，并且因为你以较慢的速度交付功能，所以更加强调与所有其他合作伙伴团队协调，以确保他们的交付功能能够解锁你的功能，因为当时的代码制作成本非常昂贵。我认为，现在有了人工智能，人工智能加速了工程设计，模型能力提高得很快，我们许多产品功能的时间表已经从六个月缩短到一个月，有时甚至缩短到一周甚至一天。因此，我们实际上需要确保产品能够快速发货。 (00:05:49)：这意味着作为产品经理，应该少强调确保你的多季度路线图与合作伙伴团队保持一致，而更多地强调，好吧，我们怎样才能找出最快的方法来推出产品？我们怎样才能弄清楚如何在我们的产品套件中创建一个概念角落，在那里我们可以……工程师有一个想法或产品经理有一个想法，到本周末，我们就能够交到用户手中。我认为在人工智能原生产品方面做得最好的产品经理能够弄清楚，如何缩短从产生这个想法到将产品实际交付到用户手中的时间，并帮助定义哪些是我的产品需要开箱即用的最重要的任务？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what I love about this is what you're saying is just like people haven't grasped how fast they need to move and how much of the job now is helping the team move fast. What helps do that? What do you do, what does your PM team do to help them move this fast other than have access to the most advanced models?
turns.zh: 所以我喜欢这个的原因是你所说的就像人们没有意识到他们需要多快的行动以及现在有多少工作正在帮助团队快速行动。什么有助于做到这一点？除了获得最先进的模型之外，您和您的 PM 团队还做了什么来帮助他们快速行动？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: I think the first thing is to set clear goals. Because LLMs are so general, that actually creates a lot of ambiguity in who we're building for, what problems we're trying to solve, what the top use cases are. And so I think a great PM is able to say, "Okay, our key user is professional developers. The main problem that we want to solve for this feature is maybe there's too many permission prompts and people are feeling fatigue, and the use case is we want professional developers at enterprises to safely get to zero permission prompts." And that actually sets a pretty clear goal because it rules out a lot of potential approaches for reducing permission prompts so that people can get a lot more done with one prompt. (00:07:42): And then I think the second thing that's very important is figuring out some repeatable process for getting these features shipped. So for Claude Code, what we do is we actually ship almost all of our features in research preview. We clearly brand this when we ship something so that users know that this is an early product, this is just an idea, this is just something that we're trying to get feedback on and iterating on, and that this might not be supported forever. And what this does is it reduces our commitment for shipping something. We can just get something out in a week or two. (00:08:17): And then the third thing that a PM should do is help create the framework for the team so that they know when to pull in cross-functional partners and what those cross-functional partners' expectations are. So for example, we have a really tight process between engineering, marketing, and docs. So when engineers have a feature that they feel is ready and that we've dogfooded internally, they post it in our evergreen launch room, and then Sarah, who leads our docs, and Alex who leads PMM, Antaric and Lydia on DevRel just jump in and can turn around the marketing announcement for it the very next day. And because we have this really tight process, it lowers the friction for any engineer to ship something, and PM is the role that should be setting this up.
turns.zh: 我认为首先是要设定明确的目标。由于法学硕士非常笼统，这实际上在我们为谁而建、我们试图解决什么问题以及最重要的用例是什么方面造成了很多模糊性。所以我认为一个优秀的 PM 能够说，“好吧，我们的关键用户是专业开发人员。我们想要解决此功能的主要问题是权限提示可能太多，人们会感到疲劳，而用例是我们希望企业的专业开发人员安全地获得零权限提示。”这实际上设定了一个非常明确的目标，因为它排除了许多减少权限提示的潜在方法，以便人们可以通过一个提示完成更多工作。 (00:07:42)：然后我认为第二件非常重要的事情是找出一些可重复的流程来交付这些功能。因此，对于 Claude Code 来说，我们所做的实际上是在研究预览中提供几乎所有功能。当我们发布某些东西时，我们会明确地品牌化这一点，以便用户知道这是一个早期产品，这只是一个想法，这只是我们试图获得反馈和迭代的东西，并且这可能不会永远得到支持。这会减少我们对运输某些东西的承诺。我们可以在一两周内得到一些东西。 (00:08:17)：PM 应该做的第三件事是帮助团队创建框架，以便他们知道何时引入跨职能合作伙伴以及这些跨职能合作伙伴的期望是什么。例如，我们在工程、营销和文档之间有一个非常严格的流程。因此，当工程师觉得某个功能已经准备就绪并且我们已经在内部进行了测试时，他们会将其发布在我们常青的发布室中，然后领导我们文档的 Sarah、以及在 DevRel 上领导 PMM、Antaric 和 Lydia 的 Alex 就会介入，并可以在第二天扭转该营销公告。因为我们有一个非常严格的流程，所以它降低了任何工程师交付产品的摩擦，而 PM 就是应该设置这个的角色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do PRDs fit into this and the fact that you said that goals are a really important part, just like being aligned on what does success look like? Who is this for? Who's this now for? Are you writing PRDs, is it just a couple bullet points? How's that evolved in the world of a PM?
turns.zh: PRD 如何适应这一点，以及您所说的目标是一个非常重要的部分这一事实，就像在成功的外观上保持一致一样？这是给谁的？现在这是给谁的？您正在写 PRD，只是几个要点吗？在 PM 的世界里这是如何演变的？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: So there's two things that we do. One is we have very rigorous metrics and we do metrics readouts with the entire team every week. The goal of this is to make sure that everyone deeply understands all the facets of our business, what our key goals are, how they're trending, and what drives them. The second thing that we do is we have this list of team principles, and this includes who our key users are, why those are our key users, and the reason that we articulate all of this is so that everybody on the team feels like they understand how our business works, they understand what's important to us and what we're willing to trade off, and it lets people make decisions by themselves without feeling like they're blocked on PM or any other stakeholder.
turns.zh: 所以我们要做两件事。一是我们有非常严格的指标，我们每周都会与整个团队一起进行指标读数。这样做的目的是确保每个人都深入了解我们业务的各个方面、我们的主要目标是什么、它们的趋势如何以及驱动它们的因素。我们做的第二件事是我们有一份团队原则清单，其中包括我们的关键用户是谁，为什么他们是我们的关键用户，以及我们阐明所有这些的原因是让团队中的每个人都觉得他们了解我们的业务如何运作，他们了解什么对我们重要以及我们愿意权衡什么，并且它让人们自己做出决定，而不会感觉他们被 PM 或任何其他利益相关者阻止。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love how so much of this is like, okay, we still need PMs in the future, and there's so much talk of why do we need PMs? We're just going to ship and build. We need engineers.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这样的感觉，好吧，我们将来仍然需要 PM，并且有很多关于我们为什么需要 PM 的讨论？我们只是要运送和建造。我们需要工程师。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Oh, we actually do PRDs sometimes. So I think for features that are particularly ambiguous, it does help to write out just a one-pager on what the goals are, what the delightful use cases are, what the failure modes currently are that we need to fix. And there are occasionally some projects, especially things that require heavy infrastructure that do take many months, and for those situations, we do write PRDs still.
turns.zh: 哦，我们有时确实会做 PRD。因此，我认为对于特别模糊的功能，写出一页纸来说明目标是什么、令人愉快的用例是什么、当前需要修复的故障模式是什么确实有帮助。偶尔会有一些项目，尤其是需要大量基础设施的项目，需要花费数月的时间，对于这些情况，我们仍然会编写 PRD。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to drill a little bit further into just how you're able to move so fast. I've never seen anything like the pace folks at Anthropic are shipping at. Someone made this calendar of launches across Anthropic, and it was literally every day there was a major feature or product. So one question people had online is you guys just launched this, not launched, but built this incredible model Mythos that is still in preview because it's so powerful, people are a little afraid of what it can do. Have you guys been using this? Is this part of the reason you've been able to move so fast?
turns.zh: 我想进一步探讨一下你是如何能够如此快速地行动的。我从来没有见过像 Anthropic 人员那样的发货速度。有人制作了整个 Anthropic 的发布日历，实际上每天都有一个主要功能或产品。因此，人们在网上提出的一个问题是，你们刚刚推出了这个，而不是推出，而是构建了这个令人难以置信的模型 Mythos，该模型仍在预览中，因为它太强大了，人们有点害怕它能做什么。大家用过这个吗？这是您能够如此快速行动的部分原因吗？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: We've been moving pretty fast for several quarters now, so I think it's not fully Mythos. Mythos is an incredibly powerful model. We do use the models internally, and I think this has increased our rate of shipping a little bit, but I don't think it explains the bulk of the increase. I think a lot of it is the process and the expectation on the team. So we're very low on process. We want to remove every single barrier to shipping things. We want to make sure every single person on the team feels empowered to take their idea from just an idea to out in the world in less than a week, sometimes even in a day.
turns.zh: 几个季度以来我们的发展速度相当快，所以我认为这并不完全是神话。 Mythos 是一个非常强大的模型。我们确实在内部使用这些模型，我认为这稍微增加了我们的发货率，但我不认为这解释了增加的大部分。我认为很大程度上是过程和对团队的期望。所以我们的流程非常少。我们希望消除运输过程中的每一个障碍。我们希望确保团队中的每个人都感到自己有能力在不到一周（有时甚至一天）的时间内将自己的想法从一个想法变成现实。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. Oh, man. What an advantage to have the best model and also be building product. That's so cool.
turns.zh: 凉爽的。哦，伙计。拥有最好的模型并构建产品是多么有利的事情。太酷了。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: We are very lucky to be able to work with the frontier models.
turns.zh: 我们非常幸运能够与前沿模型合作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh my God, what an awesome advantage, just build a thing and then use it and then accelerate faster. It's so interesting. There's a couple of these other side things, I want to just go on these sidequest on this conversation. There's so much happening with Anthropic, and I just am so curious to get your insight. One is a week ago or so, the whole source code of Claude Code leaked. Somebody got it out there. I think it was a mistake someone made. Is there anything you comment there, just like what happened? What went wrong? What should people know?
turns.zh: 天哪，这是多么棒的优势啊，只需构建一个东西，然后使用它，然后加速得更快。太有趣了。还有一些其他的事情，我想在这次谈话中继续这些支线任务。 Anthropic 发生了很多事情，我很想了解您的见解。一个是大约一周前，Claude Code 的整个源代码被泄露。有人把它拿出来了。我认为这是某人犯的错误。就像发生的事情一样，你有什么评论吗？出了什么问题？人们应该知道什么？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: So we immediately looked into this when we saw it. We realized that this was the result of human error. There was a human working with Claude to write PR. This was just an update to how we release our packages and it actually went through two layers of human review, and so this was a result of human error and we've hardened our processes to make sure that it doesn't happen in the future.
turns.zh: 所以当我们看到这个情况时，我们立即进行了调查。我们意识到这是人为错误的结果。有个人和克劳德一起写公关。这只是我们发布软件包方式的更新，它实际上经过了两层人工审核，因此这是人为错误的结果，我们强化了流程以确保将来不会发生这种情况。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is this person still at Anthropic? Are they doing all right?
turns.zh: 这个人还在人择吗？他们还好吗？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Yes, yes. It's a process failure, and the most important thing is to just learn from it and to add more safeguards so that doesn't happen again, and so that's what we've been focused on and most of those have shifted.
turns.zh: 是的，是的。这是一个流程失败，最重要的是从中吸取教训并添加更多保障措施，这样就不会再发生这种情况，这就是我们一直关注的重点，其中大部分已经发生了转变。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Another question I had is OpenClaw. So recently there's been this move to keep people from using Claude's subscription with their OpenClaws. People got really upset. They're confused why this is happening. It feels like there's harm caused to the open source community. What do people need to understand about what went into this decision?
turns.zh: 好的。我的另一个问题是 OpenClaw。因此，最近采取了一项措施，阻止人们在 OpenClaws 中使用 Claude 的订阅。人们真的很沮丧。他们很困惑为什么会发生这种情况。感觉这对开源社区造成了伤害。人们需要了解这一决定的哪些内容？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: So we've been seeing a lot of demand for Claude, and we've been working very hard to both scale our infrastructure and also to make our harness more token efficient so that you can get more usage out of it. It wasn't designed for third-party products, which have different usage patterns than our first-party ones. We spent a bunch of time trying to figure out what is the most seamless transition that we can offer, and so I was very happy to be able to say that everyone gets some credits alongside their subscription. But yeah, we did have to make the hard decision that we needed to prioritize our first-party products and our API, and so this is the decision that resulted from that.
turns.zh: 因此，我们看到了对 Claude 的大量需求，我们一直在努力扩展我们的基础设施，并提高我们的工具的代币效率，以便您可以从中获得更多使用。它不是为第三方产品设计的，第三方产品的使用模式与我们的第一方产品不同。我们花了很多时间试图弄清楚我们可以提供的最无缝的过渡是什么，所以我很高兴能够说每个人在订阅的同时都获得了一些积分。但是，是的，我们确实必须做出艰难的决定，我们需要优先考虑我们的第一方产品和 API，所以这就是由此产生的决定。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. To me, it makes so much sense. You guys are subsidizing this usage at 200 bucks a month and it's basically unlimited use of this. And I think people don't understand. Businesses are trying to make money. We're trying to be profitable here. We can't just give away compute when it's so in demand. So I get it. Coming back to the PM team, what does just the PM team look like at Anthropic? How many PMs are there? How are they kind of organized?
turns.zh: 是的。对我来说，这很有意义。你们每个月补贴 200 美元，基本上可以无限制地使用。我认为人们不理解。企业正在努力赚钱。我们正在努力在这里盈利。我们不能在如此需要计算的时候就放弃它。所以我明白了。回到 PM 团队，Anthropic 的 PM 团队是什么样的？有多少位 PM？他们是如何组织的？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Yeah, so we have a few PM teams. I think we're maybe around 30 or 40 PMs right now. So we have the research PM team who Diane leads, and this team is responsible for understanding all of the feedback from our customers for our models, and then feeding that to the best research team to act on it, and they also shepherd the model launch. There's the Claude developer platform team that maintains the APIs that Claude Code is built on top of, and they also release things like Managed Agents, which is a way for you to build your agents and we can host it on your behalf. And then there's Claude Code that works on both Claude Code and the Cowork core products. (00:15:08): There's enterprise that helps make Claude Code and Cowork easier to adopt for all of our enterprise customers, and so this is everything from cost controls, our back security controls, and just making sure that these enterprises feel very confident and comfortable using our tools. And then we also have our growth team that is responsible for growing across our entire product suite. So we work very closely with them on Claude Code and Cowork growth. And I know they also work with our other teams on CDP growth, so growth of people who use the Claude API.
turns.zh: 是的，我们有几个 PM 团队。我想我们现在可能是下午 30 或 40 点左右。因此，我们有 Diane 领导的研究 PM 团队，该团队负责了解客户对我们模型的所有反馈，然后将其反馈给最好的研究团队以采取行动，他们还负责模型的发布。 Claude 开发者平台团队负责维护 Claude Code 所构建的 API，他们还发布了诸如托管代理之类的东西，这是您构建代理的一种方式，我们可以代表您托管它。然后是 Claude Code，它适用于 Claude Code 和 Cowork 核心产品。 (00:15:08)：有些企业可以帮助我们所有的企业客户更轻松地采用 Claude Code 和 Cowork，因此这包括成本控制、后台安全控制以及确保这些企业对使用我们的工具感到非常自信和舒适的一切。然后我们还有我们的增长团队，负责我们整个产品套件的增长。因此，我们在 Claude Code 和 Cowork 发展方面与他们密切合作。我知道他们还与我们的其他团队一起致力于 CDP 的增长，以及使用 Claude API 的人员的增长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So speaking of growth, so Amol was just on the podcast. You have this really interesting insight that most people haven't been sharing. There's always this sense that we need fewer PMs in the future. Why do we need PMs? Engineers can do ship. His take is that because engineers are moving so fast, PMs and designers are squeezed. There's less time to stay on top of everything that is happening. There's a feature shipping every day. So his take is he needs more PMs because it's hard to keep up. What's your take there? Do you feel like there'll be an increase in hiring of PMs? What do you think is going on with the PM profession long-term?
turns.zh: 说到增长，阿莫尔刚刚出现在播客上。你有这个非常有趣的见解，但大多数人都没有分享过。人们总有这样的感觉：未来我们需要更少的产品经理。为什么我们需要 PM？工程师可以造船。他的看法是，由于工程师的工作节奏太快，产品经理和设计师受到了挤压。能够掌控正在发生的一切的时间越来越少。每天都有一个功能发货。所以他的看法是他需要更多的产品经理，因为很难跟上。你对此有何看法？您认为 PM 的招聘会增加吗？您认为 PM 职业的长期发展趋势如何？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: I think all of the roles are merging. PMs are doing some engineering work, engineers are doing PM work, designers are PMing and also landing code. You can either hire a lot more engineers who have great product taste, or you can keep your engineering hiring the same and hire a lot more PMs to help guide some of their work. On our team, we're pretty focused on hiring engineers with great product taste. This way, we can reduce the amount of overhead for shipping any product. There are many engineers on our team who are fully able to end to end go from see user feedback on Twitter through to ship a product at the end of the week with almost no product involvement. And this I think is actually the most efficient way to ship something. (00:17:05): So I think engineer and PM are kind of overlapping and you will get a lot of benefit from having more of either. I think product taste is still a very rare skill to have, and we'll pretty much hire anyone who we feel has demonstrated this strongly.
turns.zh: 我认为所有角色都在融合。 PM 正在做一些工程工作，工程师正在做 PM 工作，设计师正在进行 PM 并登陆代码。您可以聘请更多具有出色产品品味的工程师，也可以保持工程招聘不变并聘请更多产品经理来帮助指导他们的一些工作。在我们的团队中，我们非常注重招聘具有出色产品品味的工程师。这样，我们就可以减少运输任何产品的间接费用。我们团队中有许多工程师完全能够从在 Twitter 上查看用户反馈到在周末交付产品，几乎不需要任何产品参与。我认为这实际上是最有效的运输方式。 (00:17:05)：所以我认为工程师和产品经理有点重叠，你会从拥有更多两者中获得很多好处。我认为产品品味仍然是一项非常罕见的技能，我们几乎会雇用任何我们认为能够强烈证明这一点的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And your background was in engineering, right?
turns.zh: 你的背景是工程学，对吗？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Yeah, I was an engineer for many years. I was then a VC very briefly before joining Anthropic, and actually almost all the PMs on our team have either been engineers or ship code here on Claude Code, and so that's one of the things that I think helps build trust with the team and also just enables us to move a lot faster. And then actually our designers also have been front end engineers before.
turns.zh: 是的，我当了很多年工程师。在加入 Anthropic 之前，我曾短暂担任过 VC，实际上，我们团队中几乎所有的 PM 要么是工程师，要么是在 Claude Code 上发布代码，所以我认为这是有助于与团队建立信任的事情之一，也让我们能够更快地行动。然后其实我们的设计师以前也做过前端工程师。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Because that's the big question, there's definitely this emerging that's happening, the Venn diagrams are combining. I think the big question for a lot of people is if you're coming from engineering or product or design, which of those core skills is going to be most valuable? I could see it Anthropic and on Claude Code, engineering is very valuable. I'm curious if other companies, if you have a design background becoming a PM is more valuable or just a PM-PM.
turns.zh: 哇。因为这是一个大问题，肯定会出现这种情况，维恩图正在结合。我认为对于很多人来说，最大的问题是，如果你来自工程、产品或设计领域，那么哪些核心技能最有价值？我可以看到它是人性化的，在克劳德代码上，工程是非常有价值的。我很好奇在其他公司，如果你有设计背景，成为 PM 更有价值，还是只是 PM-PM。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: I still think it comes back to product taste. As code becomes much cheaper to write, the thing that becomes more valuable is deciding what to write. What is the right UX for this feature? What is the most delightful way that a user can experience it? We get tens of thousands of GitHub issues asking for every single thing under the sun, and it takes a lot of care and taste to figure out, okay, which of these is worth building and what is the right way to build it? And I think that skillset can come from any background, but I think that's the most important thing. (00:18:53): I think the reason why an engineering background is particularly useful, at least for the next few months, is if you have an engineering background, you have a better sense for how hard something should be, and that's often a factor in what you choose to build. So if something is very easy to build, then maybe instead of debating it, you just spend an hour doing it, but if something is harder to build and you know that upfront, then you know that, okay, this will just cost a lot more for our team to get this out the door. So it helps a bit with the prioritization.
turns.zh: 我仍然认为这又回到了产品的味道。随着代码的编写成本变得越来越低，决定编写什么内容变得更有价值。此功能的正确用户体验是什么？用户体验最愉快的方式是什么？我们收到数以万计的 GitHub 问题，询问阳光下的每一件事，需要花费大量的心思和品味才能弄清楚，好吧，其中哪些值得构建，以及构建它的正确方法是什么？我认为技能可以来自任何背景，但我认为这是最重要的。 (00:18:53)：我认为工程背景特别有用的原因是，至少在接下来的几个月里，如果你有工程背景，你就会更好地了解某件事应该有多难，而这通常是你选择构建的一个因素。因此，如果某些东西很容易构建，那么也许您不必争论它，而只需花一个小时来做​​它，但如果某些东西更难构建并且您预先知道这一点，那么您就会知道，好吧，这只会让我们的团队花费更多的成本才能将其推出。所以它对优先级排序有一点帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You said for the next few months, is that just because the models will get so good potentially in the next few months, you may not even need to know that as much?
turns.zh: 你说在接下来的几个月里，是不是因为模型在接下来的几个月里可能会变得如此优秀，你可能甚至不需要知道那么多？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: I think the valued skillsets does change quite frequently, and so it's really hard to predict more than a few months out. So it's less a commentary on what shift I think will happen and more of a commentary that I think large shifts will happen.
turns.zh: 我认为有价值的技能确实经常发生变化，因此很难预测几个月后的情况。因此，这不是对我认为将会发生什么转变的评论，而是更多关于我认为将会发生重大转变的评论。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you're not saying that's when Mythos comes out and will change everything and that we don't need to know anything about engineering?
turns.zh: 所以你不是说当神话出现时会改变一切并且我们不需要了解任何关于工程学的知识？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: No, I'm just saying that every few months it seems like there's a large increase in coding capability, which then changes what other roles are valuable. I think the most important thing is to be able to have this first principles thinking where you can figure out how the tech landscape is changing, what the team really needs from you, and to jump in and fix that hole because I think the work is becoming more amorphous, which means that a great PM is able to understand what all the gaps are to figure out what the highest priority ones are, and then to just figure out, okay, how do I learn that skillset or what is the skillset that I have that I can apply to this challenge? So I think the current environment values people who are able to wear a lot of hats, are able to swap them, and are very low ego about what work they do to help the team move faster.
turns.zh: 不，我只是说，每隔几个月，编码能力似乎就会大幅提高，从而改变其他角色的价值。我认为最重要的是能够有这个第一原则思考，你可以弄清楚技术格局正在如何变化，团队真正需要你什么，并跳入并修复这个漏洞，因为我认为工作变得越来越无定形，这意味着一个伟大的项目经理能够理解所有的差距是什么，找出最优先的差距是什么，然后弄清楚，好吧，我如何学习该技能，或者我拥有哪些技能可以应用于这个挑战？因此，我认为当前的环境重视那些能够身兼数职、能够互换职位、并且对自己所做的工作能够帮助团队更快地前进的人非常低自尊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this answer. There's this question I've been asking people in your shoes, folks that are kind of at the bleeding edge of what AI is capable of and building with the latest tools, which is just where will human brains continue to be useful and necessary for a while until we get to super intelligence. What I'm hearing here is essentially picking the things to work on, knowing where the market's going and figuring out what to prioritize essentially, and then it's knowing if the thing you've built is good and right and getting it out there in some early version at least. Does that sound right? Is there anything else of just where human brains will continue to be useful for at least the next few months?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个答案。我一直在问那些处于人工智能能力前沿并使用最新工具构建的人，这些人在我们获得超级智能之前，在一段时间内人类大脑将继续发挥作用和必要。我在这里听到的本质上是选择要做的事情，了解市场的走向，并找出本质上要优先考虑的事情，然后知道你所构建的东西是否好且正确，并至少在一些早期版本中将其推出。听起来对吗？至少在接下来的几个月里，人类大脑还有什么其他用途可以继续发挥作用吗？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: I think humans still provide a level of common sense that the models don't, and there's a thousand moving pieces to any product launch, some of them are very small, but there's always a lot that could potentially go wrong. I think the model doesn't always have a great sense of who all the stakeholders are, how they relate to each other, what their preferences are, what are the right venues to communicate with them, to keep them on board. I think a lot of this more tacit common sense EQ kind of knowledge is still very valuable. Of course, we want the models to get better at this and I think they will be, but right now I think there's still gaps.
turns.zh: 我认为人类仍然提供了模型所不具备的一定程度的常识，并且任何产品发布都有一千个移动部件，其中一些非常小，但总有很多可能会出错的地方。我认为该模型并不总是清楚地了解所有利益相关者是谁、他们彼此之间的关系、他们的偏好是什么、与他们沟通的正确场所是什么、让他们参与进来。我觉得很多这种比较默契的情商常识之类的知识还是很有价值的。当然，我们希望模型在这方面做得更好，我认为它们会的，但现在我认为仍然存在差距。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do you just deal as a human going through so much constant change, just being on the inside of the tornado, maybe it's calm there, but just like how do you stay on top of what's going on? How do you stay sane through all this craziness that we're moving through?
turns.zh: 作为一个正在经历如此多的不断变化的人类，你如何应对，只是处于龙卷风的内部，也许那里很平静，但就像你如何保持对正在发生的事情的掌控？在我们正在经历的这一切疯狂之中，你如何保持理智？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: I think our team is still people who lean into the chaos. So we try to face every challenge with a smile because there's always so much going on. There's always so many risks and tricky situations that if you get too stressed about anything, you'll burn out, and so we really look for people who can kind of look at a challenge, be like, "Whew, that's going to be hard, but I'm excited to tackle it and I'm going to do the best that I possibly can. And I know I won't be perfect, but I'll be able to sleep at night knowing that I did my best."
turns.zh: 我想我们的团队仍然是那些陷入混乱的人。因此，我们尝试微笑地面对每一个挑战，因为总会有很多事情发生。总是有很多风险和棘手的情况，如果你对任何事情压力太大，你就会精疲力尽，所以我们真的在寻找那些能够面对挑战的人，比如，“哇，这会很难，但我很高兴能解决这个问题，我会尽我所能。我知道我不会完美，但我知道我已经尽力了，晚上就能入睡。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an interesting answer to just what skills will be important in this future because it's... I forget who said this, maybe Ben Mann, that this is the most normal the world will ever be.
turns.zh: 对于未来什么技能很重要，这是一个有趣的答案，因为……我忘记是谁说的，也许是本·曼，这是世界上最正常的情况。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Yeah, it definitely gets harder. I feel like there are a lot of weeks where maybe Sunday night there's some P0 and then by Monday there's a P00 and by Monday afternoon there's a P000 and you're like, "Wow. I can't believe I was so worried about that P0 from Sunday." But I think you just have to acknowledge that there's only so much that you can do that you need to sleep well so that you can make good decisions next day and just brutally prioritize where you spend your time, what's the most important thing to get right and be okay letting things go. There's products that we ship that aren't as polished as I wish they were, but our top goal is to help empower professional developers, and if a product isn't successful, as long as it's not blocking the core use case, it's okay because we'll hear the feedback and we'll fix it in the next release. (00:24:17): Launching a feature that is buggy is the kind of thing that would have kept me up at night, but it is something that I'm now able to live with knowing that, okay, we're going to get that quick feedback and we're going to fix it in the next release.
turns.zh: 是的，这肯定会变得更难。我觉得有很多周，也许周日晚上有一些 P0，然后到周一就有 P00，到周一下午就有 P000，你会想，“哇。我不敢相信我这么担心周日的 P0。”但我认为你必须承认，你能做的事情是有限的，你需要睡个好觉，这样你才能在第二天做出正确的决定，并粗暴地优先考虑你花时间的地方，什么是最重要的事情要做对，并可以放手去做。我们发布的一些产品并不像我希望的那样完善，但我们的首要目标是帮助专业开发人员增强能力，如果产品不成功，只要它不阻碍核心用例，就没关系，因为我们会听到反馈，并会在下一个版本中修复它。 (00:24:17)：推出一个有问题的功能会让我彻夜难眠，但现在我可以忍受这个问题，因为我知道，好吧，我们将得到快速反馈，并且我们将在下一个版本中修复它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I'm imagining is there's that GIF. I think it's maybe from Pirates of the Caribbean where it's this guy walking down a pair of stairs on a ship and the whole ship is just being demolished around him and he's so chill, just strolling down the staircases as everything's falling apart. And that's interesting because everyone I've met from Anthropic is just so chill and just so optimistic. Yeah, I think that's a really interesting insight is just like having this calmness and optimism versus just like, "Oh my God, everything's crazy and going nuts."
turns.zh: 我想象的是那个 GIF。我想这可能来自《加勒比海盗》，里面有一个人走下一艘船上的楼梯，而他周围的整艘船都被拆毁了，他很冷静，只是漫步走下楼梯，而一切都在崩溃。这很有趣，因为我在 Anthropic 遇到的每个人都那么冷静、那么乐观。是的，我认为这是一个非常有趣的见解，就像拥有这种冷静和乐观，而不是“天哪，一切都疯狂了。”

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Yeah, I think if you don't have it, you'll get pretty burnt out. I think we also tend to hire people who have been in the industry for a while and have experienced lots of ups and downs and have a good sense for what gives them energy and how to maintain their energy over time, and I think that's helped us a lot.
turns.zh: 是的，我想如果你没有它，你会变得非常疲惫。我认为我们也倾向于雇用那些已经在这个行业工作了一段时间、经历过很多起起落落的人，他们对什么赋予他们能量以及如何随着时间的推移保持能量有很好的认识，我认为这对我们有很大帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So interesting. Something that I wanted to ask about is, so there's these roles blurring, engineers are becoming PMs, everyone's dogs are cats, everyone's everyone. What do we lose in that world? Do we lose career ladders and clear career paths? Do we lose design consistency, code quality? There's probably some downsides. What are some things you find are just like, okay, that's something we're sacrificing for the greater good?
turns.zh: 太有趣了。我想问的是，这些角色正在变得模糊，工程师正在成为产品经理，每个人的狗都是猫，每个人都是每个人。在那个世界里我们失去了什么？我们是否会失去职业阶梯和清晰的职业道路？我们是否会失去设计一致性和代码质量？可能有一些缺点。你发现哪些东西就像是，好吧，这是我们为了更大的利益而牺牲的东西？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: We're sacrificing product consistency. Historically, when code was expensive to write, you would carefully plan out everything in your product suite, how every product relates to each other, what the use case for every single one is, how they integrate, and you would pretty much have one product for each use case, and now with AI moving so quickly and with so many ideas that we need to test out, we do sometimes have features that overlap with each other. A lot of the times it's because there's two form factors that we love internally and we want the external audience to tell us which one is better. What that means for someone who's a new user though is a new user might not know, okay, what is the best path to accomplish X? There is more education we need to do to help people understand what the core features are and what the best practices are for using them. (00:26:41): I think this is the cost of launching a lot of features. I think users also feel like it's hard to keep up with the latest. Usually in traditional PM, you ship a feature every month or quarter, and so it's really easy for a user to understand, okay, I just need to check in on this once a month and I'll learn some new things, and if I ignore it for six months, it's fine, I don't feel like I'm missing out. I think with these agentic tools, not just Claude Code and Cowork, but across the whole ecosystem, people feel this need to check Twitter every single day to see what the absolute latest thing is, and I think there's more we can do to help people feel less like they're on this ever increasingly fast treadmill and that they feel like... I would love people to feel like they can just open these tools, the tools will educate them or teach them what they want to know, and that they can just feel more bought along.
turns.zh: 我们正在牺牲产品的一致性。从历史上看，当编写代码成本高昂时，您会仔细规划产品套件中的所有内容，每个产品如何相互关联，每个产品的用例是什么，它们如何集成，并且您几乎每个用例都有一个产品，而现在，随着人工智能发展如此之快，并且有如此多的想法需要我们测试，我们有时确实会出现彼此重叠的功能。很多时候，这是因为我们内部喜欢两种外形尺寸，并且我们希望外部观众告诉我们哪一种更好。对于新用户来说这意味着什么，尽管新用户可能不知道，好吧，完成 X 的最佳途径是什么？我们需要做更多的教育来帮助人们了解核心功能是什么以及使用它们的最佳实践是什么。 (00:26:41)：我认为这是推出很多功能的成本。我认为用户也觉得很难跟上最新动态。通常在传统的 PM 中，你每个月或每个季度发布一个功能，所以用户很容易理解，好吧，我只需要每月检查一次，我就会学到一些新东西，如果我忽略它六个月，那很好，我不觉得我错过了。我认为，有了这些代理工具，不仅仅是 Claude Code 和 Cowork，而是在整个生态系统中，人们觉得需要每天查看 Twitter，看看绝对最新的事情是什么，而且我认为我们可以做更多的事情来帮助人们感觉自己不再像在这台越来越快的跑步机上，他们感觉……我希望人们感觉他们可以打开这些工具，这些工具将教育他们或教他们他们想知道的东西，并且他们可以感觉更容易被接受。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I saw you launch this really interesting feature the other day. I think it's /powerup where it basically walks you through all the cool ways and basically all the best practices to use Claude Code. Is that kind of along these lines?
turns.zh: 是的。前几天我看到你们推出了这个非常有趣的功能。我认为 /powerup 基本上会引导您了解使用 Claude Code 的所有酷方法和基本上所有最佳实践。是这样的吗？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. So in the past, we didn't actually want to do something like powerup, because we felt like the product should be intuitive enough that you don't actually need to go through any tutorial, and over time, we've just realized that there's just so many features and there's so much demand for a built-in onboarding experience that we diverged a bit from our original principle saying no onboarding flow and added this because there's just so many users who wanted to know there's a hundred features, what are the 10 that I absolutely need to use? And so we put that together.
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。所以在过去，我们实际上并不想做像 powerup 这样的事情，因为我们觉得产品应该足够直观，你实际上不需要完成任何教程，随着时间的推移，我们刚刚意识到功能太多，而且对内置入门体验的需求太大，以至于我们偏离了我们最初的原则，即没有入门流程，并添加了这一点，因为有太多用户想知道有一百个功能，这些功能是什么10 我绝对需要使用吗？所以我们把它们放在一起。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it's such a bizarre world. So Anthropic has been really successful with B2B enterprises where traditionally you don't launch a bunch of stuff, you just kind of have quarterly release maybe, and it's like the opposite of every day we got some new... So just maybe following that thread, the run Anthropic has been on as just otherworldly. Anthropic was way behind when it started. It was, Amol shared this, just like one of the least funded companies, didn't have distribution, wasn't the first to go, OpenAI was way ahead and it was just like no way Anthropic has any chance to compete significantly long-term. Now it's just killing it, just beating the biggest companies, teams. So much just like the growth is just... $11 billion in ARR in one month growth. By the time this comes out, it'd probably be even higher. Just being on the inside, what are some ingredients that have allowed Anthropic to be this successful and kind of come from behind and do this well?
turns.zh: 是的，这就是一个多么奇怪的世界。因此，Anthropic 在 B2B 企业中确实取得了成功，传统上你不会推出一堆东西，你可能只是每季度发布一次，而这就像我们每天都会收到一些新产品的相反……所以也许沿着这条线索，Anthropic 的运行就像超凡脱俗的一样。 Anthropic刚开始时就落后了很多。 Amol 分享了这一点，就像资金最少的公司之一一样，没有分销，也不是第一个走的公司，OpenAI 遥遥领先，而且 Anthropic 没有任何机会进行长期的竞争。现在它只是杀死它，只是击败最大的公司、团队。就像增长只是......一个月的 ARR 增长 110 亿美元一样。到时候这个数字出来的时候，可能会更高。就内部而言，是什么因素让 Anthropic 取得了如此成功，并且后来居上并取得了如此出色的成绩？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: The two most important things are, one, this unifying mission. It's hard to state how important this is. We hire people who care most about bringing safe AGI to all of humanity, and this is actually something that we reference frequently in our decisions about what our entire product org should focus on shipping. And because we put this mission above any individual product line, we're able to make Make very fast decisions that cut across the entire org and execute on them in a unified way. So I think this is something that I've never seen at a company of our scale.
turns.zh: 最重要的两件事是，第一，这个统一的使命。很难说这有多重要。我们雇用最关心为全人类带来安全 AGI 的人，这实际上是我们在决定整个产品组织应重点关注的交付内容时经常引用的内容。因为我们将这一使命置于任何单个产品线之上，所以我们能够做出非常快速的决策，跨越整个组织并以统一的方式执行。所以我认为这是我在我们这种规模的公司中从未见过的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so just to make sure that's clear, so essentially having the number one mission is safety, alignment, making sure AI is good for the world, and you're saying just having that as a clear mission makes decisions a lot easier to make.
turns.zh: 因此，为了确保这一点明确，本质上，首要任务是安全、协调，确保人工智能对世界有利，你是说，只要将其作为一个明确的任务，就会更容易做出决策。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: If there's two competing priorities, we'll talk about which one is more important for Anthropic's mission, and it makes it a lot easier to decide which of the two we prioritize and then everyone will stand behind the one that we decide. And so sometimes that means that, hey, we want to ship something on Claude Code, but this other thing is more important, and so we deprioritize shipping this and we just wait until later.
turns.zh: 如果有两个相互竞争的优先事项，我们将讨论哪一个对 Anthropic 的使命更重要，这样就更容易决定我们优先考虑哪两个优先事项，然后每个人都会支持我们决定的那个。所以有时这意味着，嘿，我们想在 Claude Code 上发布一些东西，但另一件事更重要，所以我们不优先考虑这个，我们只是等到以后。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's really interesting about that is that explains, I think, versus another company maybe rhymes with OpenAI did a lot of different things, and what I'm hearing here essentially is like, okay, we're not going to launch a social network, we're not going to launch a feed of interesting information because it's not aligned to this mission, and that has kept Anthropic focused, which seems to be a core ingredient to the success.
turns.zh: 我认为真正有趣的是，与另一家公司相比，OpenAI 做了很多不同的事情，我在这里听到的基本上是，好吧，我们不会推出社交网络，我们不会推出有趣的信息源，因为它与这个使命不符，而这让 Anthropic 保持专注，这似乎是成功的核心要素。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Well, when I think about mission, I think about putting Anthropic's goals ahead of any individual org or any individual product. And so for me, it's... I think the second thing that we're very good at is focus. I think mission to me is slightly different. Mission means that teams are willing to make sacrifices that hurt their own goals and their own KRs in service of Anthropic's goals and Anthropic's KRs, and people are very happy to make those trade-offs. So an extreme example is if Claude Code failed, but Anthropic succeeded, I would be extremely happy. And the whole team is very willing to make decisions that follow that chain of thought.
turns.zh: 好吧，当我想到使命时，我会考虑将 Anthropic 的目标置于任何单个组织或任何单个产品之上。所以对我来说，...我认为我们非常擅长的第二件事是专注。我认为使命对我来说略有不同。使命意味着团队愿意为了 Anthropic 的目标和 Anthropic 的 KR 做出损害自己目标和 KR 的牺牲，并且人们非常乐意做出这些权衡。所以一个极端的例子是，如果 Claude Code 失败了，但是 Anthropic 成功了，我会非常高兴。整个团队非常愿意按照这个思路做出决策。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I don't know if you can talk about this in depth, but do you feel like the OpenClaw decision is a part of this, just like, okay, this is not furthering the mission of Anthropic, we need to stop this because it's not working in the way we want it to work?
turns.zh: 我不知道你是否能深入讨论这个问题，但你是否觉得 OpenClaw 的决定是其中的一部分，就像，好吧，这并没有推进 Anthropic 的使命，我们需要阻止它，因为它没有按照我们希望的方式工作？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: I think one of the most important things for Anthropic is to grow the number of users that we're able to reach. One of the ways that we're able to do this is with the Claude subscriptions with our first-party products. And so we just very much want to double down on that, but that does come at the expense of third-party products sometimes.
turns.zh: 我认为对于 Anthropic 来说最重要的事情之一就是增加我们能够覆盖的用户数量。我们能够做到这一点的方法之一是通过我们的第一方产品订阅 Claude。因此，我们非常想在这方面加倍努力，但这有时确实会以牺牲第三方产品为代价。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So we've been talking about Claude Cowork, all these things. Something that I want to make sure people get, and I'm curious just how you use these tools. So there's Claude Code, there's Claude desktop/web, there's Cowork. What's the best way to understand when to use which? When do you use each of these three?
turns.zh: 所以我们一直在谈论克劳德·科沃克，所有这些事情。我想确保人们得到一些东西，我很好奇你如何使用这些工具。因此，有 Claude Code、Claude 桌面/网络、Cowork。了解何时使用哪个的最佳方法是什么？你什么时候使用这三个？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: So I tend to use Claude Code in the terminal when I'm just kicking off a one-off coding task, and I want all of the latest features. The CLI is our initial product surface, and it's also the one where our features often land first, and so it's the most powerful of all the tools. So that's what I tend to use when I'm just trying to kick off one or maybe a handful of tasks at a time. I think desktop really shines when you're doing something that requires front end work, and so one thing that I love to do is to use our preview feature. (00:33:22): So if I'm building a web app, I'll often use Claude Code and desktop. I'll have the preview pane open on the right-hand side so that I can actually see the web app that I'm making in real-time as I'm chatting with Claude. It's also really great for people who want something a bit more graphical. A terminal can feel very unfamiliar to someone who's non-technical. You get a bunch of these scary popups on your machine and you can't click around the way that you're used to in pretty much every other product that you use. So there's a lot of people who just don't feel comfortable in the terminal, and if that's you, I would highly recommend checking out Claude Code on desktop. Desktop is also great for getting an at-a-glance view of everything that's happening. So you can see your CLI terminal sessions in desktop, you can see your other desktop sessions, you can see your sessions that you kicked off on web and mobile. So it's a one-stop control point where you can see all of your tasks. (00:34:16): I think the benefit of web and mobile is that it's really great for kicking things off on the go. So CLI and desktop both require you to be on your local laptop, and this is constraining because sometimes you're out and about, you're touching grass, you're going on a walk and you don't have your laptop open, and I can't count the number of people who I've seen holding their laptop open, like tethered to their phone while they're outside. And this just means that we're missing a product that solves that need. And so for me, what mobile lets you do is kick off these tasks on the go so that you don't need to bring your laptop everywhere and make sure that your laptop's open wherever you are.
turns.zh: 因此，当我刚刚开始一项一次性编码任务并且想要所有最新功能时，我倾向于在终端中使用 Claude Code。 CLI 是我们最初的产品界面，也是我们的功能通常首先落地的界面，因此它是所有工具中最强大的。因此，当我只是想一次开始一项或多项任务时，我倾向于使用这种方法。我认为当你做一些需要前端工作的事情时，桌面真的很闪耀，所以我喜欢做的一件事就是使用我们的预览功能。 (00:33:22)：所以如果我正在构建一个网络应用程序，我会经常使用 Claude Code 和桌面。我将在右侧打开预览窗格，以便在与 Claude 聊天时实际看到我正在实时制作的 Web 应用程序。对于想要更多图形化内容的人来说，它也非常有用。对于非技术人员来说，终端可能会感到非常陌生。您的计算机上会出现一堆可怕的弹出窗口，并且您无法像在您使用的几乎所有其他产品中习惯的方式单击。因此，有很多人对终端感到不舒服，如果是你，我强烈建议你查看桌面版的 Claude Code。桌面也非常适合让您一目了然地了解正在发生的一切。因此，您可以在桌面中查看 CLI 终端会话，可以查看其他桌面会话，还可以查看在 Web 和移动设备上启动的会话。因此，它是一个一站式控制点，您可以在其中查看所有任务。 (00:34:16)：我认为网络和移动设备的好处在于它非常适合在旅途中开始工作。因此，CLI 和桌面都要求您使用本地笔记本电脑，这是有限制的，因为有时您外出走动、接触草地、散步时却没有打开笔记本电脑，而且我无法统计有多少人在外出时打开笔记本电脑，就像与手机相连一样。这仅仅意味着我们缺少能够解决这一需求的产品。因此，对我来说，移动设备让您可以随时随地启动这些任务，这样您就不需要随身携带笔记本电脑，并确保无论您身在何处，笔记本电脑都可以打开。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. I've seen people on plane. It's just like such a meme now. Just I need to let this agent finish. I can't shut this down. I need WiFi.
turns.zh: 我喜欢那个。我在飞机上见过人。现在就像这样的模因。只是我需要让这位特工说完。我无法关闭它。我需要无线网络。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Exactly. And then I think for Cowork, the role that this fills is there's a lot of work that everyone does where the output isn't code. So whether that's like getting to Slack zero or inbox zero, or whether that's creating a slide deck for some customer meeting that's coming up, or whether that's writing a quick doc on what the goals of a feature are or what the launch plan for a feature is. All of these tasks produce outputs that are non-code and Cowork is best positioned for that. So the way that I split the products in my mind is if I'm building something where the output is code, I'll use Claude Code or desktop or Claude Code on mobile, and if the output is anything that's not code, I'll use Cowork for it.
turns.zh: 确切地。然后我认为对于 Cowork 来说，它所扮演的角色是每个人都会做很多工作，但输出不是代码。因此，无论是实现 Slack 零还是收件箱零，还是为即将举行的某些客户会议创建幻灯片，或者编写一份关于功能目标或功能发布计划的快速文档。所有这些任务都会产生非代码输出，而 Cowork 最适合这一点。因此，我在脑海中划分产品的方式是，如果我正在构建输出是代码的东西，我将使用 Claude Code 或桌面或移动设备上的 Claude Code，如果输出不是代码，我将使用 Cowork。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: People are just sleeping on the success that Cowork is having. It's just growing incredibly fast, and I think people still don't understand maybe what it's for. And so what if you give us a couple use cases just in your work as a PM? What are some really interesting, maybe unexpected ways you use Cowork to save you time, get more work done?
turns.zh: 人们只是沉迷于 Cowork 所取得的成功。它的增长速度令人难以置信，而且我认为人们仍然不明白它的用途。那么，如果您给我们几个您作为产品经理工作中的用例呢？您使用 Cowork 来节省时间、完成更多工作的一些真正有趣的、也许是意想不到的方式是什么？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: If you are getting started on Cowork, the first thing that you really need to do is connect all the data sources that are relevant to your role because Cowork can only do a great job if it has access to all the context that it needs to be able to curate the output for you. So what that means for me is I connected to my Google Calendar, I connected to my Slack, to my Gmail, to my Google Drive so that it just knows... It has the flexibility to find relevant context, to ask questions, to pull in threads, and this substantially improves the quality of the result. The kinds of things I use it for are like last night we have this Code with Claude conference coming up and there's a few talks that I'm giving there. (00:36:54): And one of the talks that we're doing talks about the transition of Claude Code from an assistant to a full-on agent, and one of the things that I wanted to do in this talk was to showcase all of the products that we've been shipping that enable this transition, and also to figure out, okay, what are the success stories that people have had internally that we can use as demos? (00:37:33): And so I just fed this all into Cowork. I told Cowork the narrative that I wanted to tell, and it actually just worked for an hour. It looked through Twitter to see what we launched, it looked through our evergreen launch room, it looked in our Claude Code announced channel, which is where our team posts demos of how they've been getting the most value out of Claude Code, and it synthesized all this together to this 20-page deck that I woke up to this morning and I read through it and it was like pretty good. There were a few tweaks, so I did have to give it a round of feedback. I like my slides to have extremely minimal words and it was a little too wordy, but it was far faster than what I would be able to produce. And because Cowork has access to our whole design system, it actually looks like an Anthropic designer put it together. When you visually see it, you're like, "Oh, this is incredibly polished." (00:38:29): So these are the kinds of things that are so much faster. Making this slide deck would've taken me hours, but instead it turns out a draft that is actually quite good so that I could focus on making sure that the demos are amazing that we plug into it.
turns.zh: 如果您刚开始使用 Cowork，您真正需要做的第一件事就是连接与您的角色相关的所有数据源，因为 Cowork 只有在能够访问能够为您策划输出所需的所有上下文时才能出色地完成工作。所以这对我来说意味着我连接到我的 Google 日历，我连接到我的 Slack、我的 Gmail、我的 Google Drive，这样它就知道......它可以灵活地查找相关上下文、提出问题、拉入线索，这大大提高了结果的质量。我用它做的事情就像昨晚我们即将召开 Code with Claude 会议，我将在那里进行一些演讲。 (00:36:54)：我们正在做的一次演讲讨论了 Claude Code 从助理到全面代理的转变，我在这次演讲中想做的一件事是展示我们一直在交付的实现这一转变的所有产品，并弄清楚人们内部有哪些成功故事可供我们用作演示？我已经连接了 Google Drive，也连接了 Slack。亚历克斯是我们的产品营销人员，他整理了一份草稿，列出了他认为我们应该涵盖的要点。 (00:37:33)：所以我将这些全部输入到 Cowork 中。我把我想讲的故事告诉了Cowork，结果居然只管用了一个小时。它浏览了 Twitter 来了解我们推出的产品，它浏览了我们常青的发布室，它浏览了我们的 Claude Code 宣布频道，我们的团队在该频道中发布了他们如何从 Claude Code 中获得最大价值的演示，并将所有这些综合到了这个 20 页的甲板上，我今天早上醒来看到了它，我通读了它，感觉非常好。有一些调整，所以我确实必须给它一轮反馈。我喜欢我的幻灯片的文字非常少，而且有点太罗嗦了，但它比我能够制作的要快得多。而且因为 Cowork 可以访问我们的整个设计系统，所以它实际上看起来像是一位 Anthropic 设计师将其组合在一起。当你亲眼看到它时，你会想，“哦，这真是太精致了。” (00:38:29)：所以这些事情要快得多。制作这个幻灯片需要花费我几个小时，但事实证明这是一份实际上非常好的草稿，这样我就可以专注于确保我们插入的演示令人惊叹。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This sounds like a dream come true to PMs that... Putting decks together, so annoying.
turns.zh: 对于产品经理来说，这听起来像是梦想成真……将甲板放在一起，太烦人了。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: It's so slow.
turns.zh: 太慢了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I love people will see this deck whenever you present this. This will be out in the world. Obviously it's not the one-shotted version, but you've iterated on it. So just to help people try this for themselves, so step one is connect their... What did you say? Slack. What else do you suggest they connect?
turns.zh: 我喜欢每当你展示这个牌时人们都会看到这个牌组。这将在世界上出现。显然这不是一次性版本，但您已经对其进行了迭代。所以只是为了帮助人们自己尝试这个，所以第一步就是连接他们的……你说什么？松弛。您还建议他们连接什么？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Slack, Google Calendar, Gmail, GDrive. You should connect your communications tools and where you store your source of truth data for what your team cares about, what you care about and what you're working on.
turns.zh: Slack、谷歌日历、Gmail、GDrive。您应该连接您的通信工具以及存储您的团队关心的内容、您关心的内容以及您正在处理的内容的真实数据源的位置。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. And then what was the prompt roughly that you put in there to generate this deck?
turns.zh: 好的。然后你在生成这套牌时输入的提示大概是什么？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: So I just wrote make me a slide deck for the code with Claude Conference. This is what our PMM suggested it should cover. This is the current draft that I made that I don't like. This is one that I made manually that I don't like, but I linked it. Can you start by creating a proposed outline with details? Also, make sure it doesn't overlap too much with a keynote talk, which is more important. And then Claude read a bunch of the links that I sent to it and created a proposed outline. So then I read through its proposal and all the different ideas that I had generated for what we could cover, and I just made a decision on what I wanted to actually be in the final deck, and I think this is an example of what the role of the PM still is today. (00:40:07): It's like Claude is a great brainstorming partner. It's able to synthesize a massive amount of information really quickly and present all of the possibilities to you, but the role of the PM is still to make the end decision of, okay, what should belong in the final product? So for this, what I ended up deciding was that I wanted the talk to cover the progression from making local tasks successful to making every PR green, to helping engineers land more PRs, and for each of these, which demo would be the most compelling. And then after this decision about the outline, Cowork just went off for a few hours and built the whole slide deck.
turns.zh: 所以我刚刚写了一份克劳德会议代码的幻灯片。这是我们的 PMM 建议它应该涵盖的内容。这是我目前的草稿，但我不喜欢。这是我手动制作的，我不喜欢，但我链接了它。您可以先创建一个包含详细信息的拟议大纲吗？另外，确保它不会与主题演讲重叠太多，这一点更重要。然后克劳德阅读了我发送给它的一堆链接并创建了一个提议的大纲。然后我通读了它的提案以及我为我们可以涵盖的内容而产生的所有不同想法，我刚刚决定了我实际上想在最后的甲板上做什么，我认为这是今天总理的角色仍然是什么的一个例子。 (00:40:07)：克劳德是一位出色的头脑风暴伙伴。它能够非常快速地综合大量信息并向您呈现所有可能性，但 PM 的角色仍然是做出最终决定，好吧，最终产品应该包含什么？因此，为此，我最终决定，我希望演讲涵盖从成功完成本地任务到使每个 PR 变得绿色，到帮助工程师获得更多 PR 的整个过程，以及对于其中每一个，哪个演示将是最引人注目的。在决定大纲之后，Cowork 花了几个小时构建了整个幻灯片。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is so awesome. What an awesome part of the job to not have to do anymore, and it feels like you're talking to essentially a deck designer that also has actual knowledge about what you've worked on and can make it actually the content what you want it to be, not just make it look really nice. How did you do the design system piece? How does that work? How does it know the design system of Anthropic?
turns.zh: 这太棒了。不再需要做的工作是多么棒的一部分，感觉就像你本质上是在和一个套牌设计师交谈，他也对你所做的工作有实际的了解，并且可以使其真正成为你想要的内容，而不仅仅是让它看起来非常漂亮。你是如何完成设计系统部分的？这是如何运作的？它怎么知道Anthropic的设计系统呢？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: So what I did for this is we actually already have a standardized deck that we use across all of our external engagements. turns.zh: 所以我为此所做的是，我们实际上已经有了一个标准化的平台，我们可以在所有外部活动中使用它。 And so I just gave Claude access to that, and so it's able to see what colors we use, what fonts we use, the different kinds of, what's it called, like slide formats that are possible, and so it has 20 of these example slides.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So give an example, got it. So you upload, here's our template, work from this. Yeah.
turns.zh: 那么举个例子，明白了。所以你上传，这是我们的模板，从此开始工作。是的。

turns.zh: 沿着这些思路，我一直很好奇的是，作为 Anthropic 的产品经理，你的工具堆里有哪些？显然是 Claude Code 和 Cowork 以及所有 Anthropic 工具。你还用什么？你提到的其他什么... Slack。还有别的吗？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: So my stack is pretty heavily Claude Code, Cowork and Slack. Anthropic largely runs on Slack. I feel like it's the core OS of our company. We actually have a lot of internal tools that we make. turns.zh: 所以我的技术栈主要是 Claude Code、Cowork 和 Slack。 Anthropic 很大程度上运行在 Slack 上。我觉得它是我们公司的核心操作系统。我想说，在日常工作中，我大概 30% 的时间都在突破 Cowork 和 Claude Code 的界限，这样我就能非常清楚地意识到我们不擅长什么，并且我花了很多时间与模型交谈，以了解它为什么会犯错误。我们实际上有很多自己制作的内部工具。我认为 Claude Code 真正为我们整个公司解锁的一件事是，它确实降低了制作您想要的任何自定义应用程序的障碍，因此我们看到个性化工作软件的激增，人们为自定义用例构建这些软件，而不是使用不完全适合用例的工具。

turns.en: One of the sales folks on Claude Code, he realized he was making these repetitive decks over and over and over again, and so he actually has this web app that he built with the examples of the core Claude Code decks that we know work well, so like a 101, 201 and mastering Claude Code, and then he has a way to input specific customer context that pulls from Salesforce, that pulls from Gong, that pulls from other notes so that we can customize the decks for specific customers. turns.zh: 我认为这是非常重要的通信基础设施，我认为它们很好地完成了帮助每个人获得实时更新的核心任务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, people hate on Slack, but it's really great at what it's trying to do, and the most cutting-edge teams are hooked on it. It's so interesting.
turns.zh: 是的，人们讨厌 Slack，但它确实非常擅长它所做的事情，而且最前沿的团队都对它着迷。太有趣了。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
