Cowork can help the Applied AI person research through Slack to get the latest ETA, add that to the notes so that during the customer call, the Applied AI person has the absolute latest. And these are just workflows that people are building for themselves and sharing with other people on their team.
turns.zh: 是的。然后我们还看到他们突破了 Cowork 的界限。举例来说，如果……很多人负责多个客户，并且在任何一天都可以有 5 到 10 个客户参与，所以他们经常在前一天晚上使用 Cowork 做的事情，他们会要求 Cowork 总结一下，好吧，第二天我要举行的所有客户会议是什么？这位客户向我提出了哪些要求？他们最关心的是什么？过去会议的行动项目是什么？ Cowork 将整理这份档案，简要介绍他们在下次会议中应该注意的事项。 Cowork 还可以研究答案。因此，如果客户问：“好吧，功能 X 什么时候推出？” Cowork 可以帮助应用 AI 人员通过 Slack 进行研究以获得最新的 ETA，并将其添加到注释中，以便在与客户通话期间，应用 AI 人员掌握绝对最新的信息。这些只是人们为自己构建并与团队中的其他人共享的工作流程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So cool. Something that kind of this question, this trend, I don't know, question topic comes up a lot recently, which is tokens spend exceeding people's salary where people just use AI and it costs more than how much they're making. Are there any numbers floating around Anthropic of just how much tokens spend, say, engineers spend, I don't know, a month, a day or PMs, anything like that?
turns.zh: 太酷了。类似这样的问题，这种趋势，我不知道，问题主题最近出现了很多，那就是代币花费超过了人们的工资，而人们只是使用人工智能，而且它的成本比他们赚的钱还要多。 Anthropic 是否有任何数字表明工程师花费了多少代币，我不知道，一个月，一天或 PM 之类的？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: It is clear to us that as the models get better, people delegate far more tasks to it and they spend a lot more hours in tools like Claude Code and Cowork, and so we do see the token cost per engineer or per any knowledge worker increase every time that there's a model jump or a substantial product improvement. I think it's still much lower than what the average engineer salary is, but we see the percentage increasing over time.
turns.zh: 我们很清楚，随着模型变得更好，人们会向模型委派更多的任务，并且他们会在 Claude Code 和 Cowork 等工具上花费更多的时间，因此，每次模型跳跃或产品大幅改进时，我们确实看到每个工程师或每个知识工作者的代币成本都会增加。我认为它仍然比工程师的平均工资低得多，但我们看到这个百分比随着时间的推移而增加。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's such an interesting... We talked about how you have access to the most cutting-edge models and other advantage of working Anthropic, I believe you guys have basically unlimited tokens. You can use as much as you want. Is that right?
turns.zh: 太有趣了...我们讨论了如何获得最前沿的模型以及工作 Anthropic 的其他优势，我相信你们基本上拥有无限的代币。您想用多少就用多少。是这样吗？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: We can use a lot of tokens. Some people do run into limits, so-
turns.zh: 我们可以使用很多代币。有些人确实会遇到极限，所以——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, there's a limit. Okay. Boris, shut it down. Okay. It's so interesting how many advantages come from having the most advanced model. It's such an interesting flywheel that starts to kick in.
turns.zh: 好吧，有一个限制。好的。鲍里斯，把它关掉。好的。有趣的是，拥有最先进的模型可以带来如此多的优势。这是一个非常有趣的飞轮，开始发挥作用。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: I think we also believe a lot in empowering our internal teams to build as fast as possible, and we also trust that everyone understands how much capacity that serving these models truly costs, and we trust our team to use the tokens responsibly. So it's very frowned upon to waste tokens, but we do trust individuals to make that judgment call.
turns.zh: 我认为我们也非常相信让我们的内部团队能够尽快构建，我们也相信每个人都了解为这些模型提供服务的真正成本是多少，并且我们相信我们的团队会负责任地使用代币。因此，浪费代币是非常不受欢迎的，但我们确实相信个人会做出这样的判断。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Coming back to the PM role, we talked a little bit about this, but I think this will be really interesting for people to hear. Just what I want to understand is what do you think are the emerging skills that PMs need to develop/you most look for, AI companies most look for when they're hiring PMs these days?
turns.zh: 惊人的。回到 PM 角色，我们对此进行了一些讨论，但我认为这对人们来说会非常有趣。我想了解的是，您认为 PM 需要发展的新兴技能/您最寻找的、人工智能公司现在在招聘 PM 时最寻找的新兴技能是什么？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: I think the hardest skill is being able to define what the product should look like a month from now. I think there's a lot of ambiguity in what models are capable of in that timeline and how user behavior will change, but I think there are patterns that the best PMs can see based on how users are abusing the limits of the existing product and the best PMs can sense that, can set a direction and can steadily execute towards it and change the path if the model capabilities are much better than or worse than what they'd originally expected. I think it is very hard to be the right amount of AGI-pilled because I think everyone can see this future where the models are extremely smart and can do almost everything, in which case you actually don't need that complicated a product, you can actually just have a text box again where you tell the model what you want and it's so smart that it can add any tool or add any integration that it needs to get the job done. It knows when it's uncertain, it can ask clarifying questions. (00:52:45): It's kind of very easy to build the product for the super AGI strong model. I think the hard thing is figuring out for the current model, how do you elicit the maximum capability? How do you help users go get onto the golden path? How do you guide users to interact with the model's strengths and patch its weaknesses? This skill is pretty rare.
turns.zh: 我认为最难的技能是能够定义一个月后产品应该是什么样子。我认为模型在该时间线中的能力以及用户行为将如何改变存在很多模糊性，但我认为最好的 PM 可以根据用户如何滥用现有产品的限制来看到一些模式，并且最好的 PM 可以感知到这一点，可以设定一个方向，并可以朝着这个方向稳步执行，如果模型功能比他们最初的预期好得多或差得多，则可以改变路径。我认为要达到适当的 AGI 水平是非常困难的，因为我认为每个人都可以看到这样的未来，模型非常智能，几乎可以做所有事情，在这种情况下，你实际上不需要那么复杂的产品，你实际上可以再次有一个文本框，告诉模型你想要什么，它非常智能，可以添加任何工具或添加完成工作所需的任何集成。它知道何时不确定，它可以提出澄清问题。 (00:52:45)：为超级 AGI 强模型构建产品非常容易。我认为困难的事情是弄清楚当前模型，如何获得最大能力？如何帮助用户走上黄金之路？如何引导用户与模型的优点进行交互并修补其缺点？这个技能相当罕见。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And how do you build that skill? Is it just using each... Basically understanding the limits of each model? You talked about taste, understanding, having taste into what the model maybe is capable of, what it's great and not great to at, where it's changed?
turns.zh: 你如何培养这种技能？是不是只是使用各个……基本了解各个模型的局限性？你谈到了品味、理解、品味模型的能力、它的优点和缺点、它在哪里改变了？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Think it's spending a ton of time talking and using the model. One of the things I really like to do is to ask the model to introspect on its own behaviors. So sometimes when I notice that the model does something unexpected, like for example, there's situations where the model will make a front end change and run tests, but not actually use the UI. It's actually pretty useful to ask the model to reflect on why I did this, and sometimes they'll say that, "Hey, there was something confusing in the system prompt," or, "I didn't realize that the front end verification was part of this task," Or, "Hey, I delegated the verification to this subagent and the subagent didn't do the test and I didn't check its work." A lot of times just being very curious about why the model made the decision that it did will show you what misled it so that you can fix the harness in order to close this gap. (00:54:31): The other thing that helps is to figure out who are the users who you trust the most to give you accurate feedback about the model. Usually there's a handful of people who are much better than others at articulating what makes a specific model or model harness combination good, and there's a lot of people who will give you feedback, but not everyone's feedback is as qualified. And so finding a group of those five people you trust is really important for getting very fast feedback. I think the third thing that is useful, but not everyone loves doing is building evals. You don't need to build hundreds of evals for them to be useful. Just building 10 great evals is important for helping the team quantify what the goal is and what their progress towards it is and what they're missing, and so I think evals is this underappreciated thing that more PMs, more engineers should be working on.
turns.zh: 我认为它花费了大量时间讨论和使用模型。我真正喜欢做的事情之一就是要求模型反思自己的行为。因此，有时当我注意到模型做了一些意想不到的事情时，例如，在某些情况下模型将进行前端更改并运行测试，但实际上并不使用 UI。让模型反思我这样做的原因实际上非常有用，有时他们会说，“嘿，系统提示中有一些令人困惑的东西”，或者，“我没有意识到前端验证是这个任务的一部分，”或者，“嘿，我将验证委托给这个子代理，而子代理没有做测试，我也没有检查它的工作。”很多时候，只要很好奇模型为何做出这样的决定，就会向您展示是什么误导了它，以便您可以修复线束以缩小这一差距。 (00:54:31)：另一件有帮助的事情是找出你最信任的用户，他们可以为你提供有关模型的准确反馈。通常，少数人比其他人更擅长阐明特定模型或模型线束组合的优点，并且有很多人会给您提供反馈，但并非每个人的反馈都是合格的。因此，找到一个由您信任的五个人组成的小组对于获得快速反馈非常重要。我认为第三件有用但不是每个人都喜欢做的事情是构建评估。您不需要构建数百个评估即可让它们发挥作用。仅仅构建 10 个伟大的评估对于帮助团队量化目标是什么、他们在实现目标方面取得的进展以及他们缺少什么非常重要，因此我认为评估是一个未被充分重视的事情，更多的 PM、更多的工程师应该致力于这一工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We've covered evals a bunch. There's this trend of just like, that is the future of product management's writing evals because essentially it's what does success look like. Okay, cool. Let me actually concretely define it and then we'll know. How much of your time are you spending writing evals, would you say?
turns.zh: 我们已经介绍了很多评估。有这样一种趋势，这就是产品管理写作评估的未来，因为本质上这就是成功的样子。好吧，酷。让我实际具体地定义它，然后我们就会知道。您觉得您花了多少时间来编写评估？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: I think the importance of evals varies a bit based on the feature that you're working on or what the problem you're trying to solve is. So there are a lot of folks on our team who do spend a lot of time working on evals. We have a small pod of folks who collaborate very closely with research to more precisely understand our Claude Code behaviors and what the largest areas of improvement are and trying to measure those pretty concretely. I personally jump into evals when there's a feature that I think needs a bit more product definition, and often the output of this is, "Okay, here are five evals that I made. This is how you run them. These are the ones that succeed and these are the ones that don't, and this is the prompt that I've used to increase the success rate." It varies a lot though based on the exact feature. Not every feature needs it, but I think features such as memory benefit a lot from it.
turns.zh: 我认为评估的重要性根据您正在开发的功能或您想要解决的问题而有所不同。因此，我们团队中有很多人确实花了很多时间进行评估。我们有一小群人与研究人员密切合作，以更准确地了解我们的克劳德代码行为以及最大的改进领域是什么，并尝试非常具体地衡量这些领域。当我认为某个功能需要更多的产品定义时，我个人会进行评估，通常的输出是，“好吧，这是我所做的五个评估。这就是你运行它们的方式。这些是成功的，这些是不成功的，这是我用来提高成功率的提示。”但根据具体功能，它的变化很大。并非每个功能都需要它，但我认为内存等功能可以从中受益匪浅。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This point you made about people being very good at evaluating models so interesting. It's almost like a human eval of just like, okay, they understand where it's spiking, where it's maybe lacking. Is there anyone specific that you want to shout out that's very good at this?
turns.zh: 您提到人们非常擅长评估模型，这一点非常有趣。这几乎就像人类的评估一样，好吧，他们了解哪里突出，哪里可能缺乏。您有没有特别想称赞的人在这方面非常擅长？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Two people who I think are incredible at this are, one, Amanda, who molds Claude's character. It's just such a hard role because the task is so ambiguous. Even coding is easier because you can verify the success, whereas crafting the character requires a very strong sense of conviction in who Claude should be, and I think she has an incredible ability to not only mold the character, but also to articulate what the goals are, what the character, what's successful and what's not. The other group of people who I really trust is just the Claude Code team. (00:57:46): So we often have team lunches and whenever there's a new model we're testing, one of the fastest ways for us to get feedback is to just at these team lunches, just go to every single person and just be like, "Hey, what is your vibe on the model?" And oftentimes we'll get feedback like, "Okay, this model is not fully explaining its thinking. It's too abrupt," or like, "Hey, this model just loves writing a ton of memories, but we're not sure if the memories are high quality or not," or some people will notice that, "Okay, this model loves to test itself, which is great, or this model isn't testing itself enough." So that informs what data we look at to verify, okay, is this a larger pattern? So we have a ton of data, but it is very hard to extract insights, and so the feedback from this group helps us inform, okay, what are the hypotheses we want to test, and then we're able to extract data to test that.
turns.zh: 我认为在这方面有两个令人难以置信的人，其中之一是阿曼达，她塑造了克劳德的性格。这是一个非常困难的角色，因为任务非常模糊。甚至编码也更容易，因为你可以验证成功，而塑造角色需要对克劳德应该是谁有非常强烈的信念，我认为她拥有令人难以置信的能力，不仅可以塑造角色，而且还可以阐明目标是什么，角色是什么，什么是成功的，什么是不成功的。我真正信任的另一群人就是 Claude Code 团队。 (00:57:46)：所以我们经常举办团队午餐，每当我们测试一个新模型时，获得反馈的最快方法之一就是在这些团队午餐上，去找每个人，然后问：“嘿，你对这个模型有什么看法？”通常我们会得到这样的反馈：“好吧，这个模型没有完全解释它的想法。太唐突了”，或者“嘿，这个模型就是喜欢写大量的记忆，但我们不确定这些记忆是否高质量”，或者有些人会注意到，“好吧，这个模型喜欢测试自己，这很棒，或者这个模型对自己的测试还不够。”这告诉我们要查看哪些数据来验证，好吧，这是一个更大的模式吗？因此，我们有大量数据，但很难提取见解，因此该小组的反馈可以帮助我们了解我们想要测试的假设是什么，然后我们就能够提取数据来测试它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This point you made about the character of Claude, I had Ben Mann on the podcast, co-founder, and he talked about this, just the character, the constitution of Claude is such an important part of Claude. And I didn't realize until afterwards just with OpenClaw actually, one of the reasons people are sad is the personality of your Claude is... Because Claude's personality is so good and fun and interesting unlike other models. And the way he put it is the personality is what makes Claude so good at so many things. It feels like this trivial side thing. Okay, it's going to be funny and interesting and talk in a fun way, but it's so core to the success of Claude. Is there anything get shared there about just what people may not understand about why the character, as you described, and the personality is so key?
turns.zh: 关于克劳德的性格，我在播客上提到了联合创始人本·曼（Ben Mann），他谈到了这一点，只是克劳德的性格、构成是克劳德的重要组成部分。直到后来我才意识到，实际上，就在 OpenClaw 上，人们感到悲伤的原因之一是你的克劳德的个性是……因为克劳德的个性与其他模型不同，非常好、有趣和有趣。用他的话说，正是性格使克劳德在很多事情上都如此擅长。感觉就像这种琐碎的事情。好吧，这会很有趣，而且会以一种有趣的方式谈论，但它是克劳德成功的核心。对于人们可能不理解的为什么你所描述的角色和个性如此关键，有什么可以分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: When you reflect on everyone you've worked with, there's just some people where you're like, "I really like their energy. I really like their vibe," and when people think about Claude and Claude Code, this is one of the things that people bring up the most where they just really love that Claude, it's lighthearted and fun, but it also is extremely confident at your task. People really like that Claude's low ego, and so if you tell it, "Hey, you did this thing wrong." It's truly sorry. It's like, "Oh, shoot. Thanks for telling me. Let me fix it. Let's work together." It's also very positive. So if you're feeling like, "Oh, this is an insurmountable task. I don't know how to get started," Claude is like, "Okay, it's okay. These are the steps that I think we should take. Do you want me to get started on it for you?" (01:00:28): I think part of what makes a great Coworker is this positivity, this bias towards action, this ability to give you earnest feedback, not just agreeing with every single thing that you say, and so we try to imbue this into Claude because we think it makes it a lot more enjoyable to work with.
turns.zh: 当你反思与你共事过的每个人时，你会发现有些人会说，“我真的很喜欢他们的活力。我真的很喜欢他们的氛围。”当人们想到克劳德和克劳德·科德时，这是人们提到最多的事情之一，他们真的很喜欢克劳德，它轻松愉快，很有趣，但它对你的任务也非常有信心。人们真的很喜欢克劳德的低自尊，所以如果你告诉它，“嘿，你做错了这件事。”实在是太遗憾了。就像，“哦，天哪。谢谢你告诉我。让我解决它。让我们一起努力。”这也是非常积极的。因此，如果你感觉，“哦，这是一项难以克服的任务。我不知道如何开始”，克劳德会说，“好吧，没关系。这些是我认为我们应该采取的步骤。你想让我为你开始吗？” (01:00:28)：我认为成为一名优秀同事的部分原因在于这种积极性、这种对行动的偏向、这种给你真诚反馈的能力，而不仅仅是同意你所说的每件事，所以我们试图将这一点灌输给克劳德，因为我们认为这会让合作变得更加愉快。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's something I want to come back to. You talked about how when new models come out, you often have to revisit things you've built. That's so interesting and so frustrating maybe, just like, "Oh, Goddammit it. Reshipped this thing, now I have to rethink it." Talk about just how often you have to come back with a new model and they're like, "Okay, we have to redo this product that we launched a few months ago."
turns.zh: 有件事我想回来。您谈到了当新模型出现时，您经常需要重新审视您已经构建的东西。这可能很有趣，也很令人沮丧，就像，“哦，该死的。重新发货了这个东西，现在我必须重新考虑它。”谈论您需要多久带着新型号回来时，他们会说，“好吧，我们必须重做几个月前推出的这款产品。”

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: A lot of the changes that we make with a new model is removing features that are no longer needed. So a lot of times we add features to the product as a crutch for the model because it's not naturally doing itself. So the classic example for this is the to do list. When we first launched Claude Code, people would ask it to do these larger factors and Claude Code would say, "Okay, cool. I need to change these 20 call sites," and it would go and change five of them and then stop. And then we were like, "Okay, how do we force it to remember to get every single one of these 20?" And so Sid on our team was like, "Okay, what if we just think about what a human would do? A human would make a list of everything that they need to change. Similar to how in VS Code, you would look up all the call sites and it would be a list on the left side and you would go through them one by one and replace all. How do we give this kind of a tool to Claude?" (01:01:55): And so he added the to do list and we found that with that, Claude was actually able to fix all these 20 call sites. But then with Opus 4 and later models, we realized that we didn't need to force it to use this to do list, it would naturally use itself. For the earlier models, we had to keep reminding it, "Hey, did you finish everything on the to do list? You can't finish until you're done with everything on the to do list." And for the later models, without prompting, it's just naturally thinks to do everything on the to do list. These days, the to do list is still nice to have as a user because then you can more clearly see what Claude is working on. But honestly, it's such a de-emphasized part of the product right now that the model may use it, the model may not use it. It's really not necessary for it to make thorough changes anymore.
turns.zh: 我们对新模型所做的许多更改都删除了不再需要的功能。所以很多时候我们都会向产品添加功能作为模型的拐杖，因为它本身并不是自然而然的。因此，典型的例子就是待办事项列表。当我们第一次推出 Claude Code 时，人们会要求它执行这些更大的因素，Claude Code 会说，“好吧，酷。我需要更改这 20 个调用站点”，然后它会更改其中的 5 个，然后停止。然后我们就想，“好吧，我们如何强迫它记住获取这 20 个中的每一个？”因此，我们团队中的 Sid 说：“好吧，如果我们只考虑人类会做什么呢？人类会列出他们需要更改的所有内容。类似于 VS Code 中的方式，您将查找所有调用站点，这将是左侧的一个列表，您将一一浏览它们并替换所有内容。我们如何为 Claude 提供这种工具？” (01:01:55)：所以他添加了待办事项列表，我们发现克劳德实际上能够修复所有这 20 个呼叫站点。但后来在 Opus 4 及更高版本中，我们意识到我们不需要强迫它使用这个待办事项列表，它自然会使用自己。对于早期的模型，我们必须不断提醒它，“嘿，你完成了待办事项清单上的所有内容吗？只有完成了待办事项清单上的所有内容，你才能完成。”而对于后来的型号，在没有提示的情况下，它只是自然而然地想到去做待办事项清单上的所有事情。如今，作为用户，拥有待办事项列表仍然很好，因为这样您可以更清楚地看到 Claude 正在做什么。但老实说，它现在是产品的一个不被重视的部分，模型可能会使用它，模型可能不会使用它。确实没有必要再进行彻底的改变了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I forget who said this on the podcast, that the model will eat your harness for breakfast, and what I'm hearing here is essentially you remove things over time that you've had to add on top of the model where it was not operating the way you wanted. And essentially, as the models get smarter, it becomes simpler and simpler for it just to do the thing you want it to do.
turns.zh: 我忘记是谁在播客上说过这句话了，模型会吃掉你的安全带当早餐，而我在这里听到的基本上是，随着时间的推移，你必须删除一些东西，而这些东西你必须添加到模型上，因为它没有按照你想要的方式运行。从本质上讲，随着模型变得越来越智能，它做你想做的事情就变得越来越简单。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Yeah. We can remove a lot of prompting interventions every time the model gets smarter. And we actually do this every time we launch a model, we read through the entire system prompt and we reflect on, okay, for each of these sections, does the model really need this reminder anymore, and if not, we'll remove it. The most exciting thing that new models unlocks though is just entirely new features. So there's a lot of features that we've been testing out with prior models and the accuracy wasn't high enough for us to want to launch them, and so one example of this is code review. We tried to build a code review product a few times and we've launched simpler versions of code review, which is the /codereview command in the past, and it was only with the most recent models that we felt like, okay, this code review is so good that our engineering team relies on this code review to pass before we merge PRs. (01:03:58): And we found that this was... We've always dreamed of Claude being able to be a reliable code reviewer that we can confidently feel catches the majority of bugs, and it was only with Opus 4.5 and 4.6, and Sonnet 4.6 that we felt like, okay, we are now able to run multiple code review agents simultaneously to traverse the entirety of the code base and to synthesize a set of real issues that an engineer needs to address before merge. And so this is a new capability that the newest models have unlocked.
turns.zh: 是的。每当模型变得更聪明时，我们就可以删除很多提示干预。实际上，我们每次启动模型时都会这样做，我们会通读整个系统提示，然后反思，好吧，对于每个部分，模型是否真的需要这个提醒，如果不需要，我们将删除它。新模型解锁的最令人兴奋的事情就是全新的功能。因此，我们已经使用之前的模型测试了很多功能，但准确性不够高，我们无法启动它们，因此代码审查就是一个例子。我们尝试过构建一个代码审查产品几次，并且推出了更简单版本的代码审查，也就是过去的 /codereview 命令，只有最新的模型我们才觉得，好吧，这个代码审查太好了，以至于我们的工程团队在合并 PR 之前依赖这个代码审查来通过。 (01:03:58)：我们发现这是......我们一直梦想着 Claude 能够成为一名可靠的代码审查员，我们可以自信地认为他可以捕获大多数错误，只有 Opus 4.5 和 4.6 以及 Sonnet 4.6 才让我们感觉，好吧，我们现在能够同时运行多个代码审查代理来遍历整个代码库并综合工程师需要解决的一组实际问题需要在合并之前解决。因此，这是最新型号解锁的新功能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is another trend that is very common on this podcast of build something that will possibly be possible in the next six months, be kind of at the edge of what's working sort of, and then it'll catch up and then it'll be an amazing product and you'll be ahead of everyone.
turns.zh: 这是这个播客中非常常见的另一个趋势，即构建一些可能在未来六个月内实现的东西，处于某种工作的边缘，然后它会迎头赶上，然后它将成为一个令人惊叹的产品，你将领先于所有人。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. It's pretty important to build products that don't necessarily work yet so that you know, okay, what is missing for this product to work? And then with the newest model, you can just swap it into the prototype you've already made and see, okay, does this new model close that gap?
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。构建不一定能工作的产品非常重要，这样你就知道，好吧，这个产品缺少什么才能工作？然后使用最新的模型，您可以将其替换为您已经制作的原型，然后看看这个新模型是否缩小了这一差距？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How much are you able to speak to just where things are going with Claude and Cowork as the vision of it? I imagine you don't want to give away too much about the goal, but it feels like there's all these awesome features being added on top, dispatch, control from phone and all these mobile app, all these things. What's kind of just a way to understand the vision for all these things long-term?
turns.zh: 你能在多大程度上以克劳德和科沃克为愿景来谈论事情的进展情况？我想你不想透露太多关于目标的信息，但感觉好像在上面添加了所有这些很棒的功能，调度，通过电话和所有这些移动应用程序进行控制，所有这些东西。有什么方法可以理解所有这些事情的长期愿景？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: We think about this in terms of building blocks. So for both Claude Code and Cowork, the core building block is making individual tasks successful. So you wanted to produce some output, you give it a prompt description. Is it able to consistently produce acceptable output that you're able to either merge or share with your colleagues or external audience? So the task is the core building block. As the models get smarter, the task access rate gets a lot higher, and then we see people moving towards doing multiple tasks at the same time. So multi-Claudeing was this big thing towards the end of 2025, and it's only increased since then. And so we see this as, okay, great. One task works, and now you can do six tasks at a time. As the models get even smarter, the way that we are extrapolating this is, okay, next, maybe you're going to run 50 Claudes at a time or hundreds of Claudes at a time, and so what is the infrastructure we need to build to enable that? (01:06:30): At that point, you're probably not going to run everything locally on your machine anymore. There's just not enough RAM to do it. And so we're thinking about how do we make it easier for you to manage all these? These will probably run remotely. How do we build the interface so that you as a human know which tasks you need to look into? How do we make sure that the agent is fully verifying its work so that when you look at a task and it says it's done, you can very quickly verify and fully trust that it is done to your spec. And how do we make sure that this process is self-improving so that when you do see a task that isn't done to your liking, you can give it feedback and the model will know for every future run to incorporate that feedback so it never makes that mistake again? So this is the progression that we're bringing our users along for.
turns.zh: 我们从构建模块的角度来思考这个问题。因此，对于 Claude Code 和 Cowork 来说，核心构建模块都是使单个任务取得成功。所以你想产生一些输出，你给它一个提示描述。它是否能够始终如一地产生可接受的输出，您可以将其合并或与同事或外部受众共享？所以任务是核心构建块。随着模型变得更加智能，任务访问率变得更高，然后我们看到人们开始同时执行多个任务。因此，到 2025 年底，多人克劳丁将成为一件大事，而且从那时起它的数量只会增加。所以我们认为这很好。一项任务有效，现在您可以一次执行六项任务。随着模型变得更加智能，我们推断的方式是，好吧，接下来，也许您将一次运行 50 个 Claudes 或一次运行数百个 Claudes，那么我们需要构建什么基础设施来实现这一点？ (01:06:30)：到那时，您可能不再在计算机上本地运行所有内容。只是没有足够的 RAM 来执行此操作。因此，我们正在考虑如何让您更轻松地管理所有这些？这些可能会远程运行。我们如何构建界面，以便您作为一个人知道您需要研究哪些任务？我们如何确保代理完全验证其工作，以便当您查看任务并显示其已完成时，您可以非常快速地验证并完全相信它已按照您的规范完成。我们如何确保这个过程是自我改进的，以便当您确实看到未按照您的喜好完成的任务时，您可以向其提供反馈，并且模型将知道未来的每次运行都会纳入该反馈，这样它就不会再犯同样的错误了？这就是我们为用户带来的进步。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a lot of people listening, a lot of product managers, a lot of maybe founders, a lot of other cross-functional folks listening. There's a lot of worry about just how their role... Just the future of their careers. What advice would you have for just people to not just survive this transition to this very AI-driven world, but to be really successful to essentially just to thrive in this future? What are just things people need to hear, need to be doing?
turns.zh: 有很多人在听，很多产品经理，很多可能是创始人，还有很多其他跨职能的人在听。人们对他们的角色……以及他们职业生涯的未来有很多担忧。您对人们有什么建议，让他们不仅能在这个由人工智能驱动的世界的过渡中生存下来，而且能真正成功，在未来蓬勃发展？人们需要听到、需要做的事情有哪些？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: I think AI gives everybody a ton more leverage than they used to, and so I would push you towards anytime you realize that you're doing some manual task multiple times, think about how you can use Claude Code, Cowork, or other AI tools to automate that for you. Most people have creative parts of their job that they absolutely love and then tedious parts of their job that they really hate doing. I think the beauty of AI is that it can do those tedious parts for you. It can learn from every time that you've done that manual task and generalize and then run it automatically and so that you can focus on the creative parts and that means you can do a lot more than you used to be able to do. (01:08:32): So I think my immediate push for people is figure out the repetitive parts that you can pass to Claude, iterate on those automations until the success rate is very high, and then focus on, okay, what more can you be doing for your team, for your product, for your company that people haven't had the bandwidth to pick up so far, or what is that pet project that you always thought the company should do that you've never had bandwidth to do? If AI can take care of the grunt work, then you have this extra 20% time now that you might not have before. So my push is to lean into these tools, hand off the work that you're not excited to do, figure out how it can accelerate you, and then as a result, you'll be able to do so much more.
turns.zh: 我认为人工智能给每个人带来了比以前更多的影响力，所以当你意识到自己正在多次执行某些手动任务时，我会推动你思考如何使用 Claude Code、Cowork 或其他人工智能工具来为你实现自动化。大多数人的工作中有他们非常喜欢的创造性部分，但也有他们真正讨厌做的乏味部分。我认为人工智能的美妙之处在于它可以为你完成那些繁琐的部分。它可以从您每次完成手动任务中学习并概括，然后自动运行它，以便您可以专注于创意部分，这意味着您可以做比以前更多的事情。 (01:08:32)：所以我认为我对人们的直接推动是弄清楚你可以传递给 Claude 的重复部分，迭代这些自动化，直到成功率非常高，然后专注于，好吧，你还可以为你的团队、你的产品、你的公司做哪些人们到目前为止还没有足够的带宽来完成的事情，或者什么是你一直认为公司应该做但你从来没有足够的带宽去做的宠物项目？如果 AI 可以处理繁重的工作，那么您现在将拥有以前可能没有的 20% 的额外时间。因此，我的推动力是利用这些工具，放弃那些你不感兴趣的工作，弄清楚它如何能够加速你的工作，然后，你将能够做更多的事情。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something core to what you just shared, which I fully agree with is find problems to solve with AI. There's all this potential what all these tools can do. For a lot of people, the hardest part is just like, "What should I actually do?" And what you're saying here is just pay attention to things that you are doing constantly you can automate, pay attention to just ideas that have been floating around that you haven't had time to do. It's basically it's like solve a problem for yourself is kind of the core advice there.
turns.zh: 我完全同意你刚才分享的核心内容，那就是用人工智能找到需要解决的问题。所有这些工具都具有巨大的潜力。对于很多人来说，最困难的部分就是“我实际上应该做什么？”你在这里所说的只是关注那些你经常做的、可以自动化的事情，关注那些一直流传但你没有时间做的想法。基本上，为自己解决问题就是核心建议。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Exactly. I would also push listeners towards focusing on bringing your automations from, okay, this is a cool concept to like, hey, this actually works 100% of the time. Sometimes I see users trying to automate something, getting it to 90, 95% accuracy and then giving up on it, and if an automation doesn't work 100% of the time, it's not really an automation, and that last five to 10% does take more time. Also, building the automation is often a lot slower than you doing it yourself. I would encourage listeners to put in that time to scope some automation that you really want to get to 100%, put in the elbow grease to teach Claude your preferences, to give it feedback so that it can improve its skill so that it can get to that 100%, and then really then you'll be able to rely on it. There's just not much value in a 95% there automation.
turns.zh: 确切地。我还会推动听众专注于实现自动化，好吧，这是一个很酷的概念，喜欢，嘿，这实际上 100% 的时间都有效。有时我看到用户尝试自动化某些东西，使其达到 90%、95% 的准确率，然后放弃它，如果自动化不能 100% 地工作，那么它就不是真正的自动化，而最后 5% 到 10% 确实需要更多时间。此外，构建自动化通常比您自己构建要慢得多。我鼓励听众花些时间来确定一些你真正想要达到 100% 的自动化程度，花点时间告诉 Claude 你的偏好，给它反馈，以便它可以提高其技能，从而达到 100%，然后你就真的可以依赖它了。 95% 的自动化并没有多大价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I am super guilty of that. This is really good advice for me.
turns.zh: 我对此非常内疚。这对我来说确实是一个很好的建议。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: I am guilty of this too. I've been teaching Cowork to try to get me to inbox zero for Gmail, and it has been very time-consuming and it is definitely not there as you probably realize.
turns.zh: 我也对此感到内疚。我一直在教 Cowork 尝试让我的 Gmail 收件箱为零，这非常耗时，而且您可能意识到它绝对不存在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Funny enough, that's exactly where my mind goes. I have this workflow I set up where every email I get, it looks for things that are spammy, which is just all these like, "Hey, can I come on your podcast?" Or, "What about this?" All these things, I'm just like, "I don't have time for these sorts of things," and I have it categorized it into a folder called Spammy and it's just like, it's 95% great, but then there's like, oh, wow, I missed an email because it went in there. So this is a good push for me to like, I'm going to work on this. I'm going to get it to perfect.
turns.zh: 是的。有趣的是，这正是我的想法。我设置了这样的工作流程，我收到的每封电子邮件都会查找垃圾邮件，就像“嘿，我可以加入你的播客吗？”或者，“这个怎么样？”所有这些事情，我只是想，“我没有时间做这些事情”，我把它分类到一个名为“垃圾邮件”的文件夹中，就像，它 95％ 很棒，但然后就像，哦，哇，我错过了一封电子邮件，因为它进入了那里。所以这对我来说是一个很好的推动力，我会为此努力。我要把它做到完美。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Yeah. We also are working on making the flow for customizing these commands a lot easier because right now I think you have to know too many concepts. You have to know to define a skill, you have to know to use this skill and give it feedback, and then you have to know to tell Cowork to update the skill based on all the feedback that you gave, and then you also have to know where to read the skill to make sure that the feedback was incorporated the way that you want. It's also our job to make this flow really seamless so that it doesn't feel painful to do.
turns.zh: 是的。我们还致力于使自定义这些命令的流程变得更加容易，因为现在我认为您必须了解太多概念。您必须知道如何定义一项技能，您必须知道如何使用该技能并为其提供反馈，然后您必须知道告诉 Cowork 根据您提供的所有反馈来更新该技能，然后您还必须知道在哪里阅读该技能，以确保按照您想要的方式合并反馈。我们的工作也是让这个流程真正无缝，这样做起来就不会感到痛苦。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Is there anything else, Cat, you wanted to share? Anything else you wanted to leave listeners with? Anything you wanted to double down on that we haven't already touched on before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 惊人的。猫，你还有什么想分享的吗？您还有什么想留给听众的吗？在我们进入非常激动人心的闪电回合之前，您有什么想要加倍努力但我们尚未触及的事情吗？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: I see a lot of people playing around with AI and building prototype apps and tinkering with building workflows. I would really push people towards building apps that you're actually using every single day because I think only through that usage are you actually getting the value. If you build a prototype app that isn't helping you get more done, then the AI isn't really adding value to your day.
turns.zh: 我看到很多人都在研究人工智能、构建原型应用程序以及修改构建工作流程。我真的会推动人们构建你每天实际使用的应用程序，因为我认为只有通过这种使用，你才能真正获得价值。如果您构建的原型应用程序不能帮助您完成更多工作，那么人工智能并没有真正为您的一天增加价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And there's only so much you learn from that when it's like, okay, I just did one-shotted something, oh, that's cool, and then you never come back to it. You're not learning a lot.
turns.zh: 当你觉得，好吧，我只是一次性做了一些事情，哦，那很酷，然后你就再也没有回来的时候，你从中学到的东西就只有这么多。你没有学到很多东西。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: And you're not getting much leverage from it.
turns.zh: 而且你并没有从中获得太多的影响力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And actual leverage. Yeah, that's such a good point.
turns.zh: 以及实际杠杆。是的，这是一个很好的观点。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: I also think there's a lot of people who spend a lot of time customizing their workflow. So I think there's two ends of the spectrum. One is people who never customize or never build automations, but there's this polar opposite end of people who obsess around customizing their tool, adding a ton of skills and MCPs and these workflow improvements, and I think sometimes that can even distract from your core goal of launching some product or building some feature. I think there's a lot of fun in customizing and we definitely want to make our products very hackable so that you can make it work really well for you, but there is a limit to how much it's useful, and I think there's a camp of people who maybe spend so much time customizing that they're not sleeping and not doing the core task that they originally set out to do.
turns.zh: 我还认为有很多人花了很多时间定制他们的工作流程。所以我认为有两个极端。一种是从不定制或从不构建自动化的人，但还有一种截然相反的人，他们痴迷于定制他们的工具，添加大量技能和 MCP 以及这些工作流程改进，我认为有时这甚至会分散你对推出某些产品或构建某些功能的核心目标的注意力。我认为定制有很多乐趣，我们肯定想让我们的产品非常容易破解，这样你就可以让它真正为你工作，但它的有用程度是有限的，而且我认为有一群人可能花了太多时间定制，以至于他们没有睡觉，也没有做他们最初打算做的核心任务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I see a lot of that on Twitter. Just like, "Look at my setup. It's out of control. It's so optimized," and what are you actually building? No, but my setup is so awesome. It gets so much done.
turns.zh: 我在 Twitter 上看到很多这样的内容。就像，“看看我的设置。它已经失控了。它是如此优化”，而你实际上在构建什么？不，但我的设置太棒了。它完成了这么多。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: I think the simple setups actually work better.
turns.zh: 我认为简单的设置实际上效果更好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: /powerup. Level up a little bit.
turns.zh: /通电。稍微提升一点水平。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Yeah,
turns.zh: 是的，

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. There's this Karpathy tweet that just came out yesterday where you talked about this divide that's interesting between people that tried ChatGPT, Claude back in the day, it was like, okay, and they're like, "Nah, this is terrible," and they kind of gave up on what AI could do for them and they're just so cynical of like, "No way, it's not actually that big of a deal." And then there's people that are using it to code essentially who see the full intense power of it and how good it is and people on both sides don't understand the other side and how they see the world. And so your advice is really good here to just actually use it for real things and see how good it actually has gotten.
turns.zh: 是的。昨天刚刚发布了一条 Karpathy 推文，你谈到了尝试 ChatGPT 的人们之间的这种分歧，这一点很有趣，克劳德当时的感觉是，好吧，他们会说，“不，这太糟糕了”，他们有点放弃了人工智能可以为他们做的事情，他们只是如此愤世嫉俗，“不可能，这实际上没什么大不了的。”然后，有些人本质上使用它来编码，他们看到了它的全部强大力量以及它有多么好，而双方的人都不了解另一方以及他们如何看待世界。因此，您的建议非常好，只需将其实际用于真实的事情，看看它实际上有多好。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Yeah. I think the big shift is that the 2024 generation of products were chat-based and the Claude Code generation of products is action-based, and the big aha moment people have is when Claude can just do things on your behalf. It is an amazing feeling to know that the agent is capable of doing so much more than telling you what to do. The agent can actually just do it itself, and when people feel that, I think that's the eye-opening moment.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为最大的转变是 2024 年一代的产品是基于聊天的，而 Claude Code 一代的产品是基于行动的，人们最兴奋的时刻是 Claude 可以代表你做事。知道代理能够做的不仅仅是告诉你要做什么，这是一种令人惊奇的感觉。代理实际上可以自己做这件事，当人们感觉到这一点时，我认为那就是令人大开眼界的时刻。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Shout out Chrome Extension, the Claude Code Chrome Extension, which you could just watch it doing stuff and you'd be like, "Fill out this form for me," and I'm like, "All right, here I go."
turns.zh: 大声喊出 Chrome 扩展程序，Claude Code Chrome 扩展程序，您只需看着它做事，您就会说，“帮我填写这张表格”，而我会说，“好吧，我开始了。”

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 确切地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Anything else before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 好的。在我们开始激动人心的闪电回合之前还有什么要说的吗？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: No, let's do it.
turns.zh: 不，我们就这么做吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do it. Cat, I've got five questions for you. Welcome to the Lightning Round. There's this animation that plays, I have to make sure to say it. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 我们开始做吧。猫，我有五个问题要问你。欢迎来到闪电回合。正在播放这个动画，我必须确保说出来。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: I'm ready.
turns.zh: 我准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First question, what are two or three books that you find yourself recommending most to other people?
turns.zh: 第一个问题，您发现自己最向其他人推荐的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: I really like How Asia Works. It's a story about economic development and what are the policies and governments that make long-lasting successful economies. The other books that I'm really into are The Technology Trap. So this is actually about the past few technology revolutions, so the Industrial Revolution and the Computer Revolution and how this has affected workers. The reason that I really like this is because I think there's a lot we can learn from history to make sure that this transition goes well. And maybe on a fun note, I really like Paper Menagerie. It's just a book of short stories about coming of age and AI and just self-discovery.
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢亚洲的运作方式。这是一个关于经济发展以及哪些政策和政府能够实现经济持久成功的故事。我真正喜欢的其他书是《技术陷阱》。这实际上是关于过去几次技术革命，工业革命和计算机革命以及这对工人的影响。我之所以喜欢这个，是因为我认为我们可以从历史中学到很多东西，以确保这一转变顺利进行。也许有趣的是，我真的很喜欢纸动物园。这只是一本关于成长、人工智能和自我发现的短篇故事书。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Favorite recent movie or TV show you have really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 您最近最喜欢的电影或电视节目是？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: I really like Drive to Survive. There's no deeper meaning to it. There's just something very satisfying about people being so obsessed with a singular engineering goal and just the purity of the pursuit. And I also really love Free Solo, which is about Alex Honnold climbing El Capitan without a harness, and I think similarly, it's just such a pure achievement to be able to climb this extremely challenging, dangerous route and to be able to have the mental focus to do it knowing that if you make a single mistake, you die.
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢《求生之路》。没有什么更深层次的意义。人们如此痴迷于单一的工程目标和追求的纯粹性，这是非常令人满意的。我也非常喜欢《Free Solo》，讲述的是 Alex Honnold 在没有安全带的情况下攀登 El Capitan，我认为同样，能够攀登这条极具挑战性、危险的路线，并且能够集中精神去完成它，知道如果你犯了一个错误，你就会死，这就是一项纯粹的成就。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's insane. Yeah, that movie's out of control. And it's interesting how these relate in some way to the work you do.
turns.zh: 太疯狂了。是的，那部电影已经失控了。有趣的是，这些在某种程度上与你所做的工作有什么关系。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: I actually am a rock climber, but I first watched Free Solo before I climbed rocks. And so I thought it was impressive, but I didn't understand how impressive it was. It's one of the rare movies where the more you know about it, the more you're blown away by how insane this is. The kinds of moves doing on the wall are things that I don't think I will ever be able to do in my lifetime if it were set in a gym one feet off the ground.
turns.zh: 我其实是一名攀岩爱好者，但我在攀岩之前先看了Free Solo。所以我觉得它令人印象深刻，但我不明白它有多令人印象深刻。这是一部罕见的电影，你对它了解得越多，你就越会被它的疯狂程度震惊。如果把它放在距离地面一英尺的健身房里，我认为我一生中都无法完成在墙上做的各种动作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: With a rope.
turns.zh: 用绳子。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: With a rope.
turns.zh: 用绳子。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Did you see the documentary in that other guy, the younger one that went on ice mountains?
turns.zh: 你看过另一个人的纪录片吗，那个年轻的人登上了冰山？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: I did. That one was very sad.
turns.zh: 我做到了。那个人非常悲伤。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But that was wild. Okay, favorite product you've recently discovered that you really love.
turns.zh: 但这太疯狂了。好的，您最近发现的您真正喜欢的最喜欢的产品。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: The product that has most changed my life outside of Claude products is probably Waymo. I'm a diehard Waymo user, use it twice a day, get to and from work. So the two things that I really like about it are, one, I don't feel bad if a Waymo is waiting for me, and so I feel less pressure to be right at the curbside the moment it arrives, and the second thing is I feel like it lets me be a bit more productive. When I'm in the car with another human, I typically try not to do any work calls. I feel a little rude if I'm on my laptop the whole time. But one thing I really appreciate about the Waymo is I can call into a work call. I'm not worried about someone overhearing me. I'm not worried about, "Hey, is this rude? Am I talking too loud? Do I need to ask someone to change the music?" And so I feel like this has given me back 30 minutes every day.
turns.zh: 除了 Claude 产品之外，对我的生活影响最大的产品可能就是 Waymo。我是 Waymo 的忠实用户，每天上下班时使用它两次。所以我真正喜欢它的两件事是，第一，如果 Waymo 正在等我，我不会感到难过，所以当它到达时，我感觉在路边的压力更小，第二件事是我觉得它让我更有效率。当我和另一个人在车里时，我通常会尽量不接任何工作电话。如果我一直使用笔记本电脑，我会觉得有点粗鲁。但我真正欣赏 Waymo 的一件事是我可以拨打工作电话。我并不担心有人偷听我的讲话。我不会担心“嘿，这很粗鲁吗？我说话太大声了吗？我需要请人改变音乐吗？”所以我觉得这让我每天节省了 30 分钟。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All these second order effects of technology, it's so interesting.
turns.zh: 所有这些技术的二阶效应非常有趣。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Yeah. I always saw Waymo needed to be priced lower than Uber and Lyft to succeed, but actually I'm very happy to pay a 2X premium for it.
turns.zh: 是的。我一直认为 Waymo 的定价需要低于 Uber 和 Lyft 才能成功，但实际上我很高兴为其支付 2 倍的溢价。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love Waymo. It's just like once you see it, you're just like, "This is insane." And then you get used to it. You get in there, you're like, "This is crazy," and then you forget about it.
turns.zh: 我爱韦莫。就像一旦你看到它，你就会说：“这太疯狂了。”然后你就习惯了。当你进入那里时，你会说，“这太疯狂了”，然后你就忘记了。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Totally. And I think it's also changed the vernacular. A lot of people at Anthropic love Waymo, and I think in the past you'd be like, "Hey, let's call our rideshare app," and now everyone's just like, "Okay, is Waymo here?"
turns.zh: 完全。我认为它也改变了白话。 Anthropic 的很多人都喜欢 Waymo，我想过去你会说，“嘿，让我们调用我们的拼车应用程序吧”，而现在每个人都会说，“好吧，Waymo 在这里吗？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, two more questions. Do you have a favorite life motto that you often come back to in work or in life?
turns.zh: 好吧，还有两个问题。您在工作或生活中是否有最喜欢的人生格言？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Just do things.
turns.zh: 只是做事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That tracks. That tracks.
turns.zh: 那个轨迹。那个轨迹。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: I think there's a lot of value in first principles thinking, and if you know what you're optimizing for and you have strong first principles, then you can normally deduce what the right course of action is and be able to clearly articulate that to all the stakeholders, and then you should just do it. I think jobs are fake. If you understand the constraints, you can figure out what you can do and then just try to do it quickly, learn from the mistakes and apologize or fix them if you did something wrong.
turns.zh: 我认为第一原则思考有很多价值，如果你知道你正在优化什么并且你有强有力的第一原则，那么你通常可以推断出正确的行动方针是什么，并且能够向所有利益相关者清楚地阐明这一点，然后你就应该这样做。我认为工作是假的。如果您了解这些限制，您就可以弄清楚自己可以做什么，然后尝试快速完成，从错误中吸取教训，并在做错事时道歉或修复它们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You could just do things, whoever said that.
turns.zh: 不管是谁说的，你都可以做事。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: I think it's liberating actually to tell people this. I think in a lot of companies, roles are very strictly defined like, okay, this is what the PM does, is what the designer does, this is what an engineer does, and then even team scopes are very rigidly defined. So hey, this corner of the code base we touch and this corner, we're not allowed to touch, and I think what just do things lets people do is they feel empowered to make these decisions, empowered to operate across team boundaries just to get something done.
turns.zh: 我认为告诉人们这一点实际上是一种解放。我认为在很多公司中，角色的定义非常严格，比如，好吧，这是 PM 所做的事情，这是设计师所做的事情，这是工程师所做的事情，甚至团队范围也被非常严格地定义。所以，嘿，我们触及的代码库的这个角落，以及我们不被允许触及的这个角落，我认为，让人们做的事情就是让他们感到有权做出这些决定，有权跨团队边界进行操作，只是为了完成某件事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That feels like a big important skill to be good at. People call it agency, just do the things they need to do.
turns.zh: 这感觉像是一项需要擅长的重要技能。人们称之为代理，只做他们需要做的事情。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Bias towards action.
turns.zh: 偏向行动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Bias towards action, all these ways of describing just don't wait for permission.
turns.zh: 所有这些描述方式都偏向于行动，无需等待许可。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Yeah. I think this is my favorite reason to work at a startup at some point in your life because one thing that was very life-changing for me was actually working at scale when we were 20 people, and so there was just no process and we had really big problems that we needed to solve. And I really appreciate Alex and the rest of the team for empowering me and the rest of the team to just figure things out without any boundaries for what sales supposed to do, what ops supposed to do, what engineer is supposed to do. Just like you have all the tools at your disposal, you have some ambitious hairy problem statement and you can do whatever you need to get to a good solution.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为这是我在人生中的某个时刻在初创公司工作最喜欢的原因，因为对我来说改变生活的一件事是，当我们只有 20 个人时，实际上是在大规模工作，所以没有流程，我们有真正需要解决的大问题。我真的很感谢 Alex 和团队的其他成员，他们让我和团队的其他成员能够不受任何限制地解决销售应该做什么、运营应该做什么、工程师应该做什么的问题。就像您拥有所有可供使用的工具一样，您也有一些雄心勃勃的毛茸茸的问题陈述，并且您可以采取一切必要的措施来获得良好的解决方案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You almost need that experience to build that skill to feel comfortable doing that because a lot of people, they go through school or in college and all these do the thing we tell you to do and then you will get a good grade, and you have to kind of unlearn that of like, okay, I'm just going to do the thing that needs to be done, and even if people think it's dumb, I think it's the right thing to do.
turns.zh: 你几乎需要这种经验来建立这种技能，以便感到舒服地这样做，因为很多人，他们在学校或大学里都做我们告诉你做的事情，然后你会得到一个好成绩，你必须忘记这样的事情，好吧，我只是要做需要做的事情，即使人们认为这是愚蠢的，我认为这是正确的事情。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I actually have two more quick questions, two more final questions. One is when Claude thinks there's all these, I don't know if you call them verbs, what's the term for these things?
turns.zh: 好的。实际上我还有两个简单的问题，还有两个最后的问题。一是当克劳德认为有这些的时候，我不知道你称它们为动词，这些东西的术语是什么？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Thinking words.
turns.zh: 思言。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thinking words. And interestingly, these all leaked in the source code. Do you have a favorite thinking word?
turns.zh: 思言。有趣的是，这些都在源代码中泄露了。你有最喜欢的思考词吗？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: I really like manifesting. It's also like the sticker that I have on my laptop. It's my favorite.
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢表现出来。它也像我笔记本电脑上的贴纸。这是我最喜欢的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Clearly the winner. Okay. Final question. Asked Forest this too, with AGI potentially arriving in our lifetime, when you don't potentially have to work, what are you going to do? What are you going to do with all your time?
turns.zh: 显然是赢家。好的。最后一个问题。 Forest也问了这个问题，随着AGI可能在我们有生之年到来，当你可能不需要工作时，你会做什么？你打算用你所有的时间做什么？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: I think it will take a long time for AGI to diffuse across society. So I think the immediate thing is actually just helping bring the world along. I think my non-serious answer for it after this happens is I'll probably just do a lot of rock climbing. I'll probably just live in some... I'll probably move to Fontainebleau and just live amongst 10,000 boulders and climb for a bit. There's also so many books I want to read that... My goal is to be able to read one or two books a week, and I'm currently at probably 0.5. The backlog is pretty big. I think there's just so much we can learn from history and so much that I don't understand as well as I would love to. I don't know anything about physics or robotics or any hardware or aerospace or... There's just so many interesting topics. So I'm excited to learn, even knowing that the AGI will already know it.
turns.zh: 我认为 AGI 需要很长时间才能在社会中传播。所以我认为当前最重要的事情实际上就是帮助世界进步。我想，在这件事发生之后，我对此的不严肃的回答是，我可能只会做很多攀岩运动。我可能会住在一些……我可能会搬到枫丹白露，住在 10,000 块巨石中间，然后爬一会儿。我想读的书也很多……我的目标是每周能读一两本书，目前大概是0.5。积压量相当大。我认为我们可以从历史中学到很多东西，但也有很多东西是我无法理解的。我对物理学、机器人学、硬件、航空航天等一无所知，或者……有很多有趣的话题。所以我很高兴能够学习，即使知道 AGI 已经知道了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cat, this was amazing. You're awesome. Two follow-up questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out and just follow what you're up to, and how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 猫，这太棒了。你太棒了。两个后续问题。如果人们想要联系并关注您的动态，可以在哪里找到您？听众如何对您有用？

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: The best way to reach out is I am _catwu on Twitter. Feel free to tag me in things. Feel free to DM me. I read all my DMs. I don't always respond to every single one, but I will read them all. And then the thing that is most helpful is tell us where Claude Code and Cowork aren't working well for you. We are very grateful for the amount of positive feedback, but the thing that we thrive on is edge cases, errors, like specific tasks that we can reproduce where Claude Code or Cowork fail, because if you're able to share that with us and we're able to reproduce it, then this is something that we're able to actively improve for our next generations of models and for our next harnesses.
turns.zh: 最好的联系方式是我在 Twitter 上是 _catwu。请随意在事情上标记我。请随时私信我。我阅读了所有的私信。我并不总是回复每一篇，但我会阅读它们。然后，最有帮助的是告诉我们 Claude Code 和 Cowork 哪些地方不适合您。我们非常感谢大量的积极反馈，但我们赖以发展的是边缘情况、错误，比如我们可以在 Claude Code 或 Cowork 失败的情况下重现的特定任务，因为如果您能够与我们分享这些内容并且我们能够重现它，那么我们就能够为我们的下一代模型和下一代安全带积极改进这些内容。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Extremely cool. Everyone on... People on Twitter are not shy with sharing this feedback, so keep it going.
turns.zh: 非常酷。 Twitter 上的每个人都乐于分享此反馈，所以请继续下去。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Yes, please share the problems that you're having with us.
turns.zh: 是的，请与我们分享您遇到的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, and it's really cool to see all your team being so active on Twitter and responding to people. And so what I'm hearing, this is actually stuff you guys actually see and react to.
turns.zh: 是的，看到您的所有团队在 Twitter 上如此活跃并回复人们，真是太酷了。所以我所听到的，这实际上是你们实际看到并做出反应的东西。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Yeah. We appreciate everyone being so engaged with us. It gives a team a ton of energy. We have this channel of user love, and so whenever you guys share a success story, we post it there and whenever you guys share issues with our product, we put it into our feedback channel, that way our broader team is able to act on it.
turns.zh: 是的。我们感谢每个人如此积极地参与我们的活动。它给团队带来了巨大的能量。我们有这个用户喜爱的渠道，因此每当你们分享成功故事时，我们都会将其发布在那里，每当你们分享我们产品的问题时，我们都会将其放入反馈渠道，这样我们更广泛的团队就能够采取行动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is so cool to know. Thanks for sharing that. Well, Cat, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 知道这一点真是太酷了。感谢您分享这一点。好吧，猫，非常感谢你来到这里。

turns.speaker: Cat Wu
turns.en: Thanks for having me.
turns.zh: 谢谢你有我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Bye, everyone. (01:25:11): Thank you so much for listening.
